before.approach: Park at the Cathedral Rock Trailhead (elev. ~3,350 ft) at the end of FR-4330 past Salmon La Sac, and start on the signed Cathedral Pass Trail (#1345, Okanogan-Wenatchee NF / Alpine Lakes Wilderness). The trail crosses the Cle Elum River on a footbridge near the start and enters the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary at about 0.5 mile. At roughly 2 miles, stay straight (west) at the Trail Creek Trail (#1332) junction. Squaw Lake, at 2.5 miles, is the last reliable water source and has established campsites if you're splitting the day. Beyond the lake the trail climbs through a subalpine meadow (~3.25 mi) then switchbacks up steeper, rockier tread to Cathedral Pass and the Pacific Crest Trail junction at about 4 miles (5,550 ft) — the end of maintained, signed trail. From the pass, follow the PCT west for less than half a mile to the Peggy's Pond trail junction, then take climbers' boot-paths north toward the peak, either directly up Cathedral Rock's south ridge or via the Peggy's Pond climbers' trail, crossing talus and heather benches to reach the base of the rock's main buttress/gully. Total elevation gain from the trailhead to the base of the technical climbing is roughly 2,700-3,000 ft over 4+ miles of trail, followed by a final few hundred feet of unmaintained, rocky scramble approach. Hazards: loose talus and scree on the off-trail approach, lingering seasonal snow in the entry gully into early summer (can obscure rockfall and require an axe/traction), braided undefined boot-paths near the meadows (stay on durable surfaces — this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness), and rockfall exposure from parties above once you're in the gully/buttress terrain. Stay left of the prominent South Buttress when ascending the scramble gully on the spur.

before.approach: From the Alpental parking lot, take the Snow Lake Trail; at about 1.5 miles turn off toward Source Lake. Ascend a 3rd-class rocky gully starting around 4,200 ft, reach a small cliff around 4,800 ft, traverse through a notch, then cross a snowy basin to the base of the route around 5,500 ft.
before.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb and traverse back toward the notch area, locate the marked south-facing rappel gully (the southern chimney), and make two single-rope rappels down the chimney and a third down the steep, narrow snow finger below it to return to the approach basin.

pro_tips: Combine this route with Luahna Peak (and Clark Mountain, for a full DaKobed traverse) since the approach and camp are shared.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early September, while the glacier is still well covered

July.reason: Start of the optimal window; glacier travel conditions improve through the month but bridges are still transitioning early on.

June.reason: Full snow cover and avalanche-prone conditions persist into spring; glacier crevasses are still snow-bridged, which hides rather than eliminates crevasse-fall risk, and steep-snow skills are essential.

August.reason: Core of the recommended season - glacier typically best-covered and most stable, though crevasses begin opening later in the month.

October.reason: Snow returns in fall; conditions shift toward full winter alpine and SR 20 access can become unreliable ahead of its seasonal closure.

September.reason: Early fall starts stable before snow returns - still within the recommended window but crevasses are most open and the weather window is narrowing.

before.approach: Copper Peak has no drivable trailhead — access is via the Lake Chelan ferry from Fields Point/Chelan to Lucerne Landing, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up to Holden Village (~3,300 ft) in the Railroad Creek valley, Glacier Peak Wilderness. From the village, follow the old mine road/Railroad Creek Trail east roughly 0.5 mile and cross Railroad Creek (footbridge or ford, depending on season) to reach a large tailings pile at about 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off. This climbers'/boot trail climbs steeply for about 0.7 mile up a hillside (partly burned) before entering the Copper Creek drainage, then parallels the creek south for roughly 3 miles, gaining to about 5,600 ft where it crosses a flat, open bench — this is the standard base camp (Copper Basin) used by nearly all parties. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft, but a continuing boot path pushes on toward the Copper–Entiat Divide near 7,200 ft. From camp, leave the trail, ford Copper Creek to its west side, and traverse/ascend talus and slabs alongside the outlet stream draining the Southeast Glacier remnant on the peak's east face. Reliable water is available along Railroad and Copper Creeks and near camp, but carry what you need above the basin. Hazards include two creek crossings that run higher and faster during early-season snowmelt, a steep and unmaintained burned-hillside section just above the valley floor, loose Class 3 talus/scree approaching the glacier, and real crevasse hazard on the (much-diminished but still present) Southeast Glacier — rope up for glacier travel, especially early in the season. Above the glacier a loose Class 3 gully gains a notch on the ridge's north side; a steep snowfield/snow gully beyond can require crampons and, if icy, a belay.

From the West Fork Buttermilk Trailhead (elev. ~3,960 ft, at the end of FR-4300-500 off East Buttermilk Creek Road/FR-43, reached via Twisp River Road west of Twisp), follow the West Fork Buttermilk Trail #411 into the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. The trail climbs steadily up the West Fork of Buttermilk Creek through ponderosa pine and larch forest. Expect several unbridged crossings of the creek and its side drainages that can run high and fast with snowmelt through June — plan on wet feet or careful boulder-hopping in early season. Maintenance is light and blowdowns are common in the lower miles in recent years; a GPS track is worth carrying since flagging/tread can thin out where deadfall forces detours around downed timber. At roughly 7–7.5 miles and about 3,500 ft of cumulative gain, the trail tops out at Fish Creek Pass (~7,480 ft), a major junction where it meets the Fish Creek Trail #1248; Star Lake sits just below/north of the pass and is the last reliable water source before the summit push, and a common camp for parties splitting the trip over two days. From the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up the obvious boot path/climbers' trail that switchbacks northwest up the open ridge toward Courtney Peak. This use trail gains roughly 900–1,000 ft on easy class 2 tundra and talus with a good game/climbers' path most of the way; a few hundred feet below the summit it steepens into larger class 2+ boulders that require careful hopping and some route-finding to the summit block. Snow can linger in the gullies near the pass and on the upper ridge into July, so an ice axe is worth carrying for early-season (June) attempts. Round trip from trailhead to summit and back runs about 17 miles with roughly 4,700 ft of total gain — this matches a long car-to-car day or an overnight with camp at Star Lake, not the longer Star/Oval combined traverse some parties do as a multi-summit epic.

before.descent_text: Two established options, both usually done with a single 60m rope. (1) Standard/faster — from the true summit, downclimb and simul-climb the upper West Ridge (short sections to low 5th class) west to the first set of bolted, chain rappel anchors (ASCA rebolted the route's hardware in 2010). From there, do three more single-rope rappels off bolted chain anchors — four rappels total — down the north/northwest side of the upper ridge, interspersed with short downclimbs and a traverse to regain the ridge crest. Below the last rappel, downclimb loose, exposed 3rd-class terrain and cross a scree bowl (cairns mark the line — the direct-looking line cliffs out) down to the boulder field, then retrace the approach through the meadow to the creek crossing and trailhead. Car-to-car for South Buttress via this West Ridge descent typically runs 9–10 hours. (2) Alternative — reverse the South Buttress line itself: parties who prefer to avoid the loose West Ridge traverse can rappel the buttress directly, but this takes 12 or more single-rope rappels (documented trip reports used a 70m rope) down mixed slab/chimney terrain with variable anchor quality (a mix of bolted stations and some tat/tree anchors), and takes considerably longer than option 1. Most parties choose the West Ridge descent.

before.approach: Access begins in Chelan via the Lady of the Lake passenger ferry (Lady Express ~2.5 hrs or Lady II ~4 hrs) or floatplane to the roadless village of Stehekin, then a scheduled valley shuttle bus/van up the Stehekin Valley Road to High Bridge (~1,700 ft), the trailhead for the Agnes Creek Trail/PCT and the end of the road. From High Bridge there are two documented approach options to the base of the peak: (1) Traditional Swamp Creek approach -- hike the Agnes Creek Trail (PCT) south about 5-5.5 miles to Fivemile Camp (2,200 ft), continuing about 3 more miles (roughly 8-9 miles total from High Bridge) to Swamp Creek Camp (2,800 ft); leave the maintained trail and follow the long-unmaintained, heavily brushed Swamp Creek climbers' path upvalley, crossing Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and pushing through roughly a quarter mile of thick slide alder and vine maple, to reach a lower basin (often not until after dark for many parties); continue cross-country from the lower basin to the upper basin (about 4-5 hours of further travel, reaching roughly 4,300 ft), then kick steps up around 3,000 ft of steep, often snow-covered terrain (no established track) to the saddle/col below the glacier. (2) Newer PCT/Hemlock Camp variant -- continue farther south on the PCT roughly 12.5 miles from High Bridge to Hemlock Camp, then leave the trail and climb northwest through open forest and slopes (about 3,500 ft of gain) directly to Dark Fin Col, avoiding most of the Swamp Creek brush; this is reported as a substantially easier approach even though it is not the route most published descriptions still describe as standard.
pro_tips: Consider the newer approach via the PCT to Hemlock Camp (~12.5 miles from High Bridge) and then northwest through open forest to Dark Fin Col -- multiple parties report it avoids most of the historically brutal Swamp Creek brush that most published descriptions still describe as standard.
Climb early-to-mid season (June-July) for firmer, better snow-bridged glacier conditions and to avoid the more exposed crevasses reported in late summer.
Scout the right side of the Dark Glacier, which parties often describe as the cleaner line through the crevasses.
Book the Lake Chelan ferry and Stehekin Valley shuttle well ahead of time -- the whole itinerary is built around their fixed, limited daily schedules.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-June to July, while snow smooths the upper basin and the Dark Glacier crevasses are still well bridged

May.reason: Deep snow on the approach and steep slopes below Dark Fin Col, and the valley shuttle to High Bridge runs only a limited early schedule, if at all.

July.reason: Firm styrofoam snow on the Dark Glacier with crevasses mostly covered, and the open forest approach from Hemlock Camp is snow-free.

June.reason: Steps can be kicked up the long snow slopes to the col and the glacier is firm and bridged, though the Swamp Creek brush is still wet and slow.

August.reason: Crevasses open and the summit moat grows, loose wet rock appears at the glacier margins, and wildfire can close the Agnes Creek trails.

September.reason: The glacier is bare and broken with a wide moat below the summit, and the valley shuttle and ferry move to their reduced autumn schedules.

watch_out: The Swamp Creek 'climbers path' is officially abandoned and extremely brushy; several parties have not reached the lower basin until after dark because they underestimated this leg.
The Dark Glacier is genuinely crevassed -- rope up and do not assume a given line is safe without current-condition routefinding.
The final moat/bergschrund crossing onto the summit ridge is typically the technical crux of the day and is usually belayed.
There is no cell coverage anywhere on the approach or climb; carry a satellite communicator.
The summit ridge is corniced along its entire length above the northeast face; in winter you are walking on the roof of the largest cornices in the area.
Rock outcrops and cliff bands riddle the lower slope. Getting them wrong on descent means rappelling off trees.
Slime-coated slabs near the top of the South Buttress, and mossy slabs low down on the descent.
The 65-degree notch on the old standard south-ridge line, and the short awkward step on the east-basin variation, which iced up and stopped a whole party in January.
No water on the entire route once the snow melts, on a full south aspect.
Slide alder, salal and dense young timber; one party's route through the burn-affected lower zone included heavy deadfall.
6,000 ft of steep trackless descent — the accumulated fatigue is a real hazard, not a figure of speech.
In shoulder season the slopes around Point 5872 have held avalanche-prone snow that turned parties back. Stay left (north) of it rather than committing to its slopes.
pro_tips: Go in late spring. Snow suppresses the brush, snowmelt supplies the water this slope does not have, and the avalanche hazard on the south side is minimal.

Study the map before you leave the car. Every account stresses route-finding through the rock outcrops; one party made it up without backtracking through a combination of careful map study and, in their own words, blind luck.
Above the 5,720+ ft saddle the line is about 200 ft of slab up to the sharp ridge that leads to the summit. In good snow that is step-kicking. Bare, it is class 4 and worth a rope.
The 65-degree notch on the ridge is the reason the southwest face variation exists. If steep snow is not your thing, take the SW face instead.
Take the south ridge crest on descent, not the east-basin variation. The step into the saddle looks worse than it is and has all the ledges you need.
The summit crest is the top of very large cornices overhanging the northeast face — the biggest wall in the state. Walk well back from the edge, especially in flat light.
Do not confuse this with the Davis Peak near Cle Elum, which has a maintained trail. This one does not, and never has.

before.approach: Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead (~2,360 ft) on the Mountain Loop Highway, where the pavement ends. Walk the gated road/trail roughly 1 mile to the signed junction for the Weden Creek (Gothic Basin) Trail #724, branching right off the old railroad grade. The trail climbs steeply and steadily through timber via switchbacks, fording Weden Creek about 1 mile in (the crossing can be a wet, rock-hop affair in early season or after rain). About 1.2 miles past the creek crossing (roughly 3 miles from the trailhead), the trail crosses a steep avalanche/snow gully that runs as a cascading waterfall in summer but can hold a firm, consequential snow tongue well into July — this is the trail's main hazard and can require an ice axe or careful kick-stepping in early season. Above treeline the trail breaks into subalpine meadows and rock slabs of Gothic Basin (~5,000 ft); tread carefully off-trail here as the meadows are fragile and use rock/gravel where possible. From the basin, follow the boot path past a small tarn and up boulder/talus slopes to Foggy Lake (~5,200 ft, about 4.7 miles from the trailhead) — the lake is a reliable water source (filter before drinking) and the last easy flat camping/staging area. From Foggy Lake, cross the boulder field on climbers' trail along the lake's north side, then ascend Del Campo's south-facing slopes toward ~6,200 ft, aiming for the main summit gully. Route-finding caution: the obvious gully looks like the natural line but ends in a vertical wall — the actual route exits the gully and moves onto class 3-4 rock just left of it about 100 vertical feet below the top, working up to a notch/col at roughly 6,350 ft. From the col, turn west/left and scramble the final short pitch to the true summit (6,610-6,615 ft). Total is about 11-14 miles round trip, depending on the exact approach line, with roughly 4,200-4,300 ft of gain to the summit; snow can linger in the gully and basin into early September, and a helmet is strongly recommended for the loose upper rock.

before.descent_text: From the top of the third couloir, a short snow scramble reaches the summit. Traverse to the true summit, then make a long descending traverse across the upper snowfields toward Asgard Pass, and descend the pass's gully back to the frozen/open lake and the approach trail.

before.approach: Drive the Beckler River Road (FR-65) out of Skykomish and follow it into the FR-6510/FR-6514/FR-6517 spur network (about 10.8 miles of gravel/dirt forest road past the pavement) to road's end, roughly 0.5 mile east of Eagle Rock's summit at about 4,150 ft — this is the trailhead; there is no maintained trail beyond it. From the parking area, leave the road and head west/southwest straight up the hillside cross-country. You break out of brush and into open forest within the first few hundred feet, then continue uphill through timber; after a few hundred yards the trees give way to open talus slopes below the cliff bands on Eagle Rock's northeast side. From the base of the talus, do not push straight up into the cliffs — instead make an ascending, counterclockwise (climber's-left) traverse across and around the north side of the peak to a broad bench/step at roughly 5,000 ft. From that step, angle southwest a few hundred yards to the base of the final summit slope, where the scramble proper begins. One-way distance from the car to the summit is only about 0.8 mile, but essentially all of the route's ~1,400 ft of gain is packed into that short distance, so it feels considerably steeper than the mileage implies. There is no reliable water source anywhere on the approach — carry all the water you need from the car. Hazards are mostly footing and route-finding: loose talus and scree on the traverse, brush low down, no trail or cairns to follow, and cliff bands that will cliff out parties who try to go straight up the northeast talus instead of arcing counterclockwise.
pro_tips: Identify the correct gully/ramp on the north side before committing — the right side is easier Class 2, the center/left is Class 2/3 and more exposed
Bring a map/GPS track for the NE-to-N counterclockwise talus traverse; it's easy to end up on the wrong side of the cliffs in the forest
Call the Skykomish Ranger Station or check MBS current-conditions page for FR65/6510/6514/6517 status before driving — these spur roads see periodic washout/shoulder damage
Carry a 50 ft handline for the exposed Class 3 downclimb on the north side rather than downclimbing it unroped
Best after the north-facing summit gully clears of snow for secure scrambling
before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. From the summit, downclimb the same Class 2 (right side) or Class 2/3 (center) slope back down about 600 vertical feet to the ~5,000 ft bench, then reverse the counterclockwise talus traverse below the cliff bands back to treeline, and continue down through open forest and brush to the FR-6517 parking area. No technical anchors or rappels are needed on the standard line. The main descent hazards are loose talus/scree (easy to kick rocks onto anyone below) and route-finding — in poor visibility it's easy to drift toward the cliff bands instead of holding the correct counterclockwise line, so retrace your ascent traverse carefully. Parties who climbed the more exposed far-left finish (about 50 ft of slightly exposed Class 3) sometimes downclimb that section more cautiously or carry ~50 ft of rope to rig an optional handline for extra security, but this is a personal-comfort choice on a minor variation, not a fixed rappel station, and the standard Class 2/3 line requires no rope at all.

watch_out: The direct line over Elephant Butte involves a short overhung 5th-class move — not advisable with an overnight pack
The bypass around the peak is brushy, mossy, and cliffy with genuine route-finding difficulty; some parties report getting off-route into 'horror-story' cliffy micro-terrain
The Sourdough Creek crossing is beyond the ridge turn-off on the lookout trail; if you reach it, turn back and look for the junction

before.approach: Primary approach: from Entiat, drive Entiat River Road ~32.5 miles to Forest Road 5606, then ~3 switchbacking miles to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (~3,940 ft); hike NF Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley and leave the trail to gain the west-side gully below Emerald's summit block. Alternate approach: from Lucerne on Lake Chelan (reached by boat/ferry), hike the Emerald Park Trail #1230 up into Emerald Park and approach the peak's west side from there.
watch_out: Steep slab near the south summit with real exposure toward the East Face
Erosion-loosened rock throughout the gully
The two summits are close but distinct — confirm which (north, slightly higher) is the true high point
Don't mistake the SW sub-summit (a distinctly harder, very exposed fourth-class scramble about 1,500 ft away) for this route's destination, the true NE summit
The ridge has a couple of minor humps that can cause route-finding hesitation in flat light or fog

before.descent_text: From the East Peak summit, down-climb/scramble south down talus and scree for roughly 400-500 ft, then traverse gradually south across slopes to intersect the De Roux Creek Trail and follow it down toward the De Roux trailhead. That trailhead is about a mile down the valley from the road-end Esmeralda/Ingalls trailhead where you started, so finish by walking back up the valley along the North Fork Teanaway road or the unmarked path beside it — effectively a loop rather than a reversal of the ascent gully.
pro_tips: The crux comes low, in the first ~500 ft of gully — the reverse of many alpine routes where the hard climbing is up high.
A short chimney on climber's right offers an escape from the wettest, loosest part of the main gully.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through October, with August-September as the most reliable stretch

July.reason: The valley trail and scree slope are generally clear by mid-July but lingering snow patches from the prior winter can still be present early in the month; thunderstorm season is active

August.reason: Prime dry-season conditions; watch for afternoon storm buildup

October.reason: Excellent and clear, but early-season snow is possible later in the month, especially at higher sub-summits

September.reason: Cool, clear, stable east-slope weather; one of the best months

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to late September, when the talus is snow-free and dry and the larches turn late in the month

July.reason: Snow lingers on the approach benches into early July and the summit can be wintry, but most talus melts out by late month.

June.reason: Snow covers the benches toward the Enigma saddle and the upper Castle Creek gully, and the upper talus is still snowbound.

August.reason: Benches and talus are mostly snow-free, Bird Creek Camp has water, and long days suit the cross-country round trip.

October.reason: Talus stays dry in a clear spell, but first snows can glaze the loose slope and Stehekin valley transport runs a reduced schedule.

September.reason: Settled weather and dry talus make the loose gneiss easier going; late-month larches draw visitors to the valley.

watch_out: loose rock and rubble underfoot
getting misrouted too high or too low on the ledges

pro_tips: Climb the East Ridge and descend the West Ridge for a classic traverse.
Move efficiently and simul-climb the moderate crest.
Know the West Ridge descent before committing.
Start early to stay ahead of weather on the long ridge.
before.descent_text: The East Ridge is not reversed as a rappel line in its own right; two descents are used instead. The standard one is the East Ledges, dropping climber's-right/northeast directly off the summit: three rappels trend northeast from the summit area, then a short, exposed grassy traverse east to the next rock rib, followed by two more rappels onto the East Ledges proper, about 5 rappels in all. From there, several hundred metres of loose, sandy and grassy class 3–4 ledges and slabs, marked by intermittent and sometimes doubled cairn lines, lead east above the cliffs over the crevassed Boston Glacier to a gully about 100 ft below the Solitary Gendarme; go up and over the East Ridge through it, then down snow slopes on the south side to the small glacier below Forbidden's south face and the walk back across Boston Basin. The alternative is to reverse along the ridge crest past the gendarmes to the West Ridge notch and descend the West Ridge line: about three rappels on the ridge and about five down the Cat Scratch gullies, roughly eight on a single 60 m rope. It is longer, but it is more travelled and easier to follow, and many parties prefer it to the East Ledges, which are faster but loose, exposed, rockfall-prone and easy to lose. Either way, expect mostly natural slung-horn and block anchors with some tat and a handful of fixed or bolted stations, and carry a 60 m rope.

watch_out: A short but genuinely exposed 4th-class step guards the final summit block -- check holds carefully.
The col-crossing snow slope steepens noticeably near the top and has required crampons/axe even in late-season conditions.
Route-finding through the upper Chiwawa Basin meadows and deadfall is nontrivial off-trail terrain.
before.approach: From Trinity Trailhead, hike the Buck Creek Trail about 1.4 mi to the Chiwawa River Trail (#1550), then follow it north up the valley, staying left at the Red Mountain junction near 5 mi, to a ford of the Chiwawa River; beyond it a faint path leads to an avalanche chute, and open forest climbs cross-country to a basin near 5,500 ft and a bench near 6,300 ft, then traverse diagonally up toward Chiwawa Mountain's east ridge, descending to the roughly 7,200 ft col between Chiwawa and Fortress (or continuing over Chiwawa's summit first). Some parties instead approach via the Red Mountain Trail and Chiwawa Basin. From the col, a loose class 3-4 gully gains the crest of Fortress's East Ridge.
pro_tips: Rock quality improves noticeably once you gain the East Ridge crest itself -- the approach gully below it is the loosest section.
Carry crampons and an ice axe even in late summer; parties have needed firm snow skills for the traverse across to the col.
The route is often linked with Chiwawa Mountain via the shared 7,200 ft col, making a Chiwawa-Fortress traverse or double-summit day popular.
Trekking poles help on the scree/talus benches below the ridge.
what_to_bring: Map/compass or GPS for cross-country basin travel
ice axe and crampons — snow crossing to the col

watch_out: Notoriously loose, rotten rock throughout the upper mountain -- test every hold.
Persistent snow patches below the summit block can linger into midsummer, sometimes requiring an ice axe even in July/August.
Afternoon thunderstorms build quickly over the Glacier Peak Wilderness in summer.
The way-trail past Buck Creek Pass to Pass No Pass is rough and unmaintained -- easy to lose under early-season snow.
pro_tips: The direct southwest face gully holds the loosest rock on the route; several parties recommend angling right onto slabbier class 3 rock or following the south ridge crest instead.
A cairned class 3 line over blocky terrain to skier's right of the ascent gully (found by a 2015 party) avoids some of the worst loose rock on descent.
Space climbers out (one party used a 20-minute gap) when ascending or descending the gully to reduce rockfall risk to those below.
Wear real boots, not trail runners -- parties note the scree and wet grass chew through soft footwear.
Fortress is very commonly combined with Buck Mountain and/or Chiwawa Mountain from the same Buck Creek Pass / Pass No Pass camp.
before.descent_text: From the summit, retrace the ascent line down the south ridge / upper southwest face. The direct gully is the loosest ground on the mountain; a 2015 party found and cairned an alternate class 3 line over more solid, blocky terrain to skier's right of the gully that later parties have followed. Continue down through scree and talus to the grassy benches above Pass No Pass, back over the pass, and down the Buck Creek Trail to Trinity Trailhead.

pro_tips: Commonly paired with North Ingalls Peak's south ridge for a two-summit day
Early-season snow makes for a fast glissade descent; by late summer the same slope is looser talus/scree
watch_out: Firm morning snow can require crampons even where the slope looks moderate
Rockfall/loose-talus hazard increases as the slope melts out later in summer
The gully/ridge down to the Lake Ann pass is steep and can hold snow into midsummer
Esmeralda Trailhead parking fills early — it's shared with heavy Lake Ingalls/Mount Stuart traffic
Some direct lines involve loose, exposed scrambling (T4, approaching T5 on the Mountaineers' scramble scale)

before.approach: Four Brothers sits on Chikamin Ridge in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and the standard approach starts at the Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331, ~2,375 ft), reached via SR 903 north from Cle Elum ~17 mi, then Cooper Lake Rd/FR-46 roughly 9-10 mi to the signed trailhead. From the trailhead the trail drops briefly to a crossing of the Kachess River, then climbs to a junction with the Little Kachess Trail (#1312) at about 0.25 mi. Around 1.3 mi it passes an old mine site and shortly after crosses Mineral Creek itself, entering the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary. The next stretch runs high above the creek through old-growth forest and several brushy former avalanche paths - expect deadfall and slow going here, especially early season. Near the 4-mile mark the trail crosses a side creek (the last dependable water before the basin) and then climbs steeply, gaining roughly 1,500 ft in the final mile-plus to Upper Park Lake (~4,900 ft, about 5.4 mi from the trailhead). From the Park Lakes basin, leave the trail and go cross-country up mixed heather benches and slabby rock toward the saddle on Chikamin Ridge - the four cliffy summit points of the Four Brothers are unmistakable and form steep, technical terrain that should be flanked rather than climbed directly from below. Once on the ridge crest, traverse back to the base of the southwest-facing gully/slope system that gives this route its name, roughly 6.5-7 mi and about 4,000 ft of gain from the car. Expect lingering snow in the gully well into July, loose stacked talus higher up, and real routefinding complexity picking a line through the pinnacle/cliff-band maze - this is the part of the outing that most often proves the crux, more so than any single move.
watch_out: loose footing
confusing summit cluster
pro_tips: Identify the highest brother before committing
Combine with neighboring peaks
The south peak's summit block eases from class 3 to a class 4 move depending on the crack/ledge chosen — rope up if class 4 isn't comfortable unroped.
before.descent_text: Most parties reverse the ascent line: down the southwest gully/heather slopes back to the Chikamin Ridge saddle, then back around the Four Brothers' cliff bands into the Park Lakes basin and out the Mineral Creek Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb - no fixed rappel stations are documented on the Southwest Route itself, and parties who stay on the described line generally do not need to rope up for the descent. Treat any exposed Class 3 downclimbing sections with care, particularly on wet or lichen-covered rock, and a short handline (30-60 ft) is a reasonable option for a party uncomfortable downclimbing the crux step. Note that the adjacent, better-documented Chikamin Peak has a known single-rope bail rappel off its summit horn used by parties who prefer not to downclimb its Class 3 chimney; that anchor is on Chikamin's line, not this route, but if you drift onto that terrain by mistake it's a known escape option. Because Four Brothers' summit block is a genuine cluster of cliffy pinnacles, poor visibility or late-day descent meaningfully raises the chance of wandering onto steeper terrain than intended - budget enough daylight to descend the correct gully rather than improvising a line off the pinnacles.

pro_tips: Follow the white pyroclastic aggregate band specifically — it is solid and abrasive, much like an artificial climbing wall, compared to the looser dark rock around it.
Hold a consistent traverse elevation (~7,500 ft) with your party to avoid knocking rock down onto teammates below.
Goat paths along the Goat Ribs/Goat Ledges are a useful route-finding aid.
watch_out: The route is explicitly described by experienced parties as loose and dangerous off the recommended line.
The 'black prow' rock tower and surrounding terrain are loose volcanic breccia — test holds before weighting them.
Wildfire smoke has reduced visibility on this traverse in past (Aug/Sept) seasons.
A short, exposed 'no-fall zone' step onto the true summit — a slip here is consequential despite the low technical grade.
Loose scree and talus on the approach gully can be tedious and prone to kicking rocks onto parties below.
Snowfields on Cutthroat and Granite Pass can persist into August and may require an ice axe.
Groups larger than about 6 increase rockfall risk to each other on the loose gully.
pro_tips: Camp at Upper Snowy Lake for the shortest, most direct position below Golden Horn (and Mount Hardy).
If visiting during larch season (late Sept–early Oct), arrive at the trailhead Friday evening — weekend parking fills fast.
The crux move is short but exposed over real air; even confident scramblers often protect it with a quick hip belay or toprope.
Combine with Tower Mountain (and optionally Mount Hardy) from the same Snowy Lakes camp for an efficient multi-summit trip.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking
overnight backpacking/camping gear for Snowy Lakes
water treatment (lake water available at camp)
bear canister recommended for food storage
layers for exposed, high-elevation ridge walking
ice axe — recommended for the Cutthroat/Granite Pass snowfields that can linger into August
crampons — early season, Cutthroat/Granite Pass snowfields

watch_out: Loose blocks in the final gully — test holds before weighting them, and be mindful of parties above/below.
The direct ridge variant (bypassing the gully) has real exposure with class 3–4 moves — not a place for inexperienced scramblers.
A moat can open between snow and rock right at the summit block late in the season.
before.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line — the correct SE-ridge descent is generally easier to pick out looking downhill than it was on the way up, and most parties who wandered onto the harder Class 4 rock on the ascent spot the easier Class 3 bypass ('sidewalk' ledge) on the way down. From the true summit, downclimb the short (~100 vertical foot) summit block via its broken south-side terrain rather than traversing climber's-left, which dead-ends above the exposed south face in sustained 4th-class ground. Continue down the scree/talus on the north side of the SE ridge crest (the climber's-right side on the way up) back to the Foggy Lake outlet on the same cairned line used on the ascent, then retrace the maintained Gothic Basin trail — through the basin meadows, the steep timbered switchback band, and the Weeden Creek ford — back to the Barlow Pass trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no rappelling required in normal summer conditions. The real hazards are loose rock and fall exposure on the summit block and upper scree, and, in early-season or wet/icy conditions, hard snow on the slabs and snowfield just below the ridge, where an ice axe (and caution on the creek crossing) is warranted. A short handline is occasionally carried by conservative parties for the final summit-block downclimb, but it is not standard gear for this route.

watch_out: Do not attempt the exposed connecting ledge in wet or rainy conditions — reduced friction on this narrow, sloping traverse has turned back parties.
Rockfall risk in the scree/talus gullies below Dumbell's south ridge, especially with other parties above.
Route-finding to the correct 7,900 ft notch is easy to get wrong in poor visibility — aim specifically for the notch on the southeast ridge to the right of Dumbell's summit.
before.approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft, Wenatchee River Ranger District), follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north, entering the Glacier Peak Wilderness at 2.6 miles, to Spider Meadow (about 4.5-5 miles from the trailhead). Continue past Spider Meadow on the climbers' path, staying right of the tumbling creek to scramble up slabs past waterfalls, then continue up grass, talus, and heather slopes trending northeast into upper Phelps Basin. A commonly used bivy sits around 5,700-5,800 ft near treeline with stream access (the basin above 6,000 ft often has only snow-patch camping).

From Monroe, drive east on US-2 to the town of Baring. Near milepost 41-42, across from a convenience store, turn left (north) onto 635th Place NE. Cross the railroad tracks and continue about 0.3 mile to a junction; keep left on 635th Place NE for another 0.1 mile, where the road becomes Forest Road 6024 (Barclay Creek Road). Continue roughly 3.9-4.3 miles of gravel forest road (watch for potholes and rough patches; AWD/4x4 recommended after wet weather) to the Barclay Lake Trailhead (vault toilet on site, parking for roughly 20 vehicles, Northwest Forest Pass required). From a spur road near the trailhead, follow the spur toward an old fire pit, where a faint, mostly-unmarked climber's path heads east into the forest and begins the ascent proper.
pro_tips: Occasional flagging/ribbons mark parts of the climber's path, but don't rely on them exclusively — the route is genuinely unmarked in places.
The waterfall gully crossing is easiest and driest in late summer (roughly August-September) when flow is minimal.

Gunnshy Peak is frequently confused with neighboring Gunn Peak (6,240'-6,244', about 0.7 mile east and slightly higher) — the peak visible from Gold Bar, Sultan, Monroe, and Everett is Gunnshy, not Gunn.
Snow can linger in the Gunn Lake basin well into summer; check recent trip reports before committing to the summer/fall (Gunn Lake) variation versus the winter/spring buttress-bypass variation.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, when the waterfall gully runs low or dry and the upper slabs and heather are free of snow

May.reason: The waterfall gully crossing runs high over slick rock, and the upper basin and slabs are still avalanche-prone snow.

July.reason: The creek and gully drop and most upper snow melts, though late snow patches remain on the slabs and brush is at its thickest.

June.reason: Snowmelt keeps the gully crossing and Barclay Creek high, and snow lingers on the upper slabs and summit approach.

August.reason: The waterfall gully is typically low or dry and the heather, talus and slabs to the summit are snow-free.

October.reason: Fall rain makes the mossy path and slick gully rock hazardous, and early snow patches settle on the upper slabs and exposed summit block.

September.reason: Dry gully, snow-free scrambling and cooler temperatures for the steep, brushy climber's path.

before.approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,200 ft, end of FS Rd 6024 out of Baring) do not follow the maintained Barclay Lake Trail #1055; instead walk back down the access road roughly a quarter mile and pick up the old, deactivated Barclay Creek spur road (parties who know the route often park directly at the spur's gated start rather than the main Barclay Lake lot). Follow the old roadbed about 100-200 yards to a fire-pit clearing, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden 'Gunn climbers' path.' The path drops to Barclay Creek and crosses via a log-jam/rock-hop near the downstream tip of a small mid-channel island — this ford is the approach's main early-season hazard, since the crossing can run high and slick with spring runoff. On the far bank the boot path swings west then turns north and starts climbing in earnest: about 200 ft of easier grade gives way to sustained, tight switchbacks gaining roughly 1,500 ft through second-growth timber with generally good tree/root holds underfoot but a steep, sometimes loose tread. Around 3,600-3,800 ft the path forks near a band of exposed rock — stay right and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, a known route-finding trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band in partial shade. A usually-dry waterfall ravine is crossed around 4,400 ft (can carry meltwater and be slick in early season). The trail continues switchbacking up brushy, sometimes slide-alder-choked terrain for another ~1,500 ft to gain the ridge crest at roughly 5,400 ft — call it 3-4 hours and about 3,200 ft of gain above the creek crossing for a fit party. From the ridge crest, drop about 100 ft off the crest to skirt a cliff band, then boulder-hop roughly 500 ft up a talus basin to the upper tree benches directly below the peak's south face, which marks the base of the summit scrambling. There is no reliable water above Barclay Creek/the waterfall ravine in late summer, so fill up early. Cairns thin out badly above treeline and the boot path fades in the talus, so route-finding (not technical difficulty) is the main hazard on the upper approach — carrying a GPS track or recent trip-report beta is strongly recommended.
watch_out: heavy brush on the approach
exposure near the top
pro_tips: The exposed summit ramp becomes dangerous when wet — avoid climbing it during or right after rain.
Many parties link Gunn Peak with neighboring Tailgunner Peak via the connecting ridge and a small tarn near Tailgunner Pass.
The climbers' path beyond the old logging road is unmaintained and easy to lose; a GPS track or prior route beta is strongly recommended.

watch_out: loose rock
routefinding
parties above
pro_tips: Great quick alpine rock outing thanks to the short approach
Watch for loose rock and other parties above you

before.approach: From Alpental Ski Area parking lot (3,120 ft), reach the talus cone below the west face by a line that stays off the private Alpental Community Club roads; the 'Strasse' roads off the access road are closed to walking and driving, and no established path exists. Approach time ~30 minutes to 1 hour from parking.
what_to_bring: Water (minimum 2-3L due to altitude and exposure)
Headlamp (long approach in summer daylight, but plan for changes)

watch_out: Rock quality is intermittent — test holds carefully, especially in the dihedral and gullies.
The descent is not a clean rappel line; expect downclimbing and route-finding to the SE Couloir.
Winter ascents encounter cornices near the summit and require crampons/axe.
pro_tips: The approach passes directly by the Blood Sport crag, so it's easy to combine a quick single-pitch warm-up on the way in.
Simul-climbing the upper dirt/tree/talus gully sections saves significant time.

watch_out: Loose rock and a steep dropoff to one side along parts of the ridge traverse.
Severe mosquitoes are commonly reported until mid-summer on the meadow sections.
pro_tips: Cougar Divide's trailhead sits notably higher (~4,900 ft) than Skyline Divide's, making this the shorter and less-crowded of the two standard approaches.
FS Road 33 is gated seasonally (closed roughly Nov 1-Jul 7 for wildlife protection) — confirm the gate is open before driving out.
The actual trailhead is reported to be roughly a kilometer beyond where mapping apps typically route drivers along FS 33 — don't stop early.
Route sees enough summer weekend traffic to bottleneck — start early.
The pitch-6 crux is a long reach for the ridge off a fist jam; taller climbers find it easier.
watch_out: Loose blocks in the lower gully and on belay ledges — test holds and be mindful of parties below.
Afternoon thunderstorms are common on the East Cascades crest in summer.
what_to_bring: Extra water (dry approach and route in late summer)

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July to early September, once the talus gully to the notch has melted out and the serpentine is dry

May.reason: Late May ascents happen, but the approach gully is full snow, hard in the morning and prone to wet slides as it warms.

July.reason: Snow in the gully shrinks to short patches and the slick serpentine dries; the Ingalls Way trailhead lot fills early on weekends.

June.reason: Regularly climbed: the gully holds snow needing axe and crampons early, then good plunge-stepping; the upper ridge rock is usually dry by late June.

August.reason: Snow-free loose talus to the notch and dry rock; more parties above in the gully raises rockfall risk, so start early.

October.reason: Early snow and verglas on the serpentine make the squeeze and downclimbs treacherous, and the rappel descent slows in cold.

September.reason: Larches turn and crowds peak on the Ingalls Way trail; dry rock but shorter days on a long 14-16 hour outing.

before.approach: Same trailhead and initial trail as the South Ridge: Esmeralda Basin/Ingalls Lake Trailhead, Ingalls Way Trail (#1390), ~3 miles to Ingalls Pass, then traverse to Lake Ingalls (~4-4.5 miles, ~2,500 ft gain) as described for the South Ridge. From the lake, the East Ridge approach diverges: hike around the lake's left (west/north) side and cross a band of slabs to reach a large talus gully that runs fairly directly up to the saddle/notch separating the east ridge of North Ingalls Peak from East Ingalls Peak (a boot path is intermittently visible in the talus). This gully-and-saddle approach is steeper and looser than the South Ridge's slab approach, so expect more class 2-3 scree/talus travel with some loose rock hazard, especially with parties above. At the saddle, many climbers stash approach gear (extra shoes, poles) in a small cave/nook just below the notch. The route itself starts roughly 30 feet below the saddle on its east side, marked by slings on the first anchor. As with the South Ridge, water is available at Lake Ingalls but not beyond it, and the open talus slopes carry afternoon-storm and loose-rock exposure - climb early and be alert for parties above dislodging rock in the gully.

watch_out: Pitch 1 splitter can be over-protected easily; careful placement is key
Pitches 11-15 are deceptively committing despite lower grade
Descent route-finding is critical in semi-wild terrain
before.approach: Park at the pullout where SR-20 crosses Silver Star Creek near milepost 171, about 8.5 miles east of Washington Pass. A good climbers' trail follows the east side of the creek for a couple of miles, then crosses it and climbs talus and forest up the western edge of the valley toward Juno Tower; at about 5,000 ft a rising traverse leftward threads most of the slide alder to the foot of the east prow. The usual way down is the Burgundy Col trail to the Wine Spires pullout near milepost 166, farther west on the highway: from Burgundy Col (~7,720 ft) it drops to a basin/camp bench around 6,500 ft (good camping and a late-season spring near 6,400-6,500 ft), descends the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, crosses Early Winters Creek on a log (~4,080 ft) past a trail register, and climbs a short loose talus/scree slope back up to the road.

pro_tips: Use the newer (post-July 2023) approach variation that breaks right onto yellow-flagged treed ledges before the fixed lines — noticeably less loose rock and exposure than the original approach.
Bring approach shoes; the scrambling transitions between pitches are widely reported as unpleasant in rock shoes.
The optional 7th pitch (a #3-cam crack left of the gully) and the finishing 'Goldie Crack' are frequently cited as the route's best climbing.
Start the rappel descent while there's still plenty of daylight — ropes commonly tangle on flakes and multiple parties have needed to re-ascend to free them.
before.approach: From the pullout, an unmarked but well-worn climbers' trail drops steeply from the west/southwest end of the turnout through loose dirt and rock into the trees, marked intermittently by cairns. The path crosses Early Winters Creek (on logs) before climbing into an open rocky drainage/talus below the formation; the final approach to the base involves loose 3rd/4th-class slabs, with sandy access ledges and a fixed rope on parts of the standard line.
watch_out: The start of pitch 1 is not obvious and route-finding mistakes here have led to a serious accident (a documented 2018 fall).
The descent gully is loose and 'gnarly'; stay high and skier's-right to reduce exposure to loose rock.
Cracks are frequently dirt-filled even where the surrounding rock is solid.
No reliable cell service — carry a satellite messenger.
before.descent_text: Most parties rappel the line of the route, which some report takes a long time (about 9 rappels, with occasional rope snags on flakes requiring re-ascent to free them). The alternative is descending the 3rd-class gully climber's right of the route, which is faster but described as loose and 'gnarly' — staying high and skier's-right reduces exposure to looseness.
what_to_bring: Approach shoes for the scrambling between pitches
Extra cord/rap rings for tat replacement on retreat
Water — little to none available on route

before.approach: Two primary approaches: (1) From the Cutthroat Lake trailhead on Highway 20, hike 1.8 miles with 500 feet elevation gain to Cutthroat Lake (4,800 ft). Continue another 3.7 miles with 1,800 feet elevation gain to Cutthroat Pass (6,800 ft), then follow the ridge crest south approximately 1 mile to the base of the North Ridge. (2) From Rainy Pass North trailhead (4,875 ft) on the PCT, hike about 1.5 miles north to just before Porcupine Creek (around 5,250 ft elevation), then ascend the ridge northeast toward Molar Tooth—approximately 2 miles with 2,300 feet elevation gain. The second gully provides a cleaner approach to the base of the north ridge and west rib.
watch_out: Loose rock and rockfall hazard—constant vigilance on gully approaches and between pitches
Coarse granite with poor quality sections between technical pitches
Limited protection on some traverse sections; place pieces conservatively
Descending in low light with loose rock creates serious hazard—plan descent before dark
Vertical granite can be slick when damp or icy early season
Open crevasses and weak snow bridges on the upper Emmons
Avalanche slab in the Corridor after fresh snow/wind
Crevasses on the Inter Glacier during descent glissades
Heat and soft snow on the long afternoon exit
pro_tips: Go early season (June) for the most filled-in, direct line
Rope up on the Inter Glacier too — it has caught people out late season
Camp Schurman fills on summer weekends; reserve ahead
Watch the Corridor for wind slab after storms
what_to_bring: stove for melting water at Schurman

pro_tips: Move efficiently — simul-climbing the easy ground saves hours
Study the False Summit area; route-finding here trips people up
Combine West Ridge ascent with Cascadian descent for a clean loop
Start early for the long approach + ridge + descent
before.descent_text: Descend via the Cascadian Couloir, the standard walk-off for the entire Stuart massif — this is a scramble descent, not a rappel route, under normal (dry to firm-snow) conditions. From the summit, reverse the short 3rd/2nd-class scramble east along the summit ridge to the false summit (~9,200 ft), then drop into the broken rock and scree above the top of the couloir. Stay climber's-right through sparse trees and rock bands near the top to find the true couloir entrance rather than dropping into parallel gullies to the left, which cliff out. From there it's a sustained, direct descent of loose scree/talus (snow early season) losing about 4,000 ft to the floor of the Ingalls Creek valley — many parties glissade or boot-ski the upper snowfield when it's in, which is markedly faster and easier on the knees than the bare-scree version later in summer. Watch for sun cups and inconsistent snow texture on the upper couloir, and expect significant rockfall exposure funneled by the gully, especially with other parties above or below. At the bottom, pick up a climber's path through meadows to the Ingalls Creek Trail near the Longs Pass turnoff, then reverse the approach (back over Longs Pass) to the Esmeralda Trailhead. No rappels are required on this descent in normal conditions; a fixed/natural rock anchor has been reported near the false summit that some parties use to rappel the initial short, steep, icy step off the summit ridge in early-season or verglassed conditions, but this is a discretionary variation, not a standard part of the descent, and the anchor is not maintained or guaranteed. Total summit-to-trailhead time is commonly 3–5 hours for a fit party in good conditions.

pro_tips: Most parties bypass the Great Gendarme via a short rappel rather than climb it direct — decide before you're below it
The traverse gully below the Gendarme can hold snow/ice into midsummer
Bring rock shoes (or at least a stiff approach shoe) just for the crux offwidth/crack pitch — most of the rest goes fine in approach shoes.
Check every old rappel sling/anchor before weighting it — the rock is loose and slings degrade fast in this weather.
Climbing later in summer (August) reduces the glacier/moat crossing hazard below the ridge but exposes more loose rock; earlier season means more snow/crampon travel on the approach gully.
Plan on 3 days (hike in, climb+bivy at the col, hike out) rather than trying it in a single big day — the approach alone is long and physical.
A park-wide fixed-anchor moratorium is in effect in North Cascades National Park wilderness — do not place new bolts; rely on natural protection and existing tat.
before.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb roughly 30 ft off the north side of the notch to easier rock, then reverse the ridge via a long string of rappels (double-rope where two ropes are carried) interspersed with downclimbing — accounts report anywhere from about 7 to 10 rappels total, including a double-rope rappel off the crux crack pitch — back down to the bivy col. Existing slings and rap rings are present at most stations but the rock is loose, so back up or replace suspect anchors. From the col, reverse the approach gully and climbers' path back around Thornton Lake and out the Thornton Lakes Trail to the trailhead.

Don't confuse Walkinshaw's gully with neighboring Needles gullies — many look similar from below
Wear a helmet for the whole climb; parties above dislodge rock easily

watch_out: Chossy rock on the single technical pitch

Route-finding from Jefferson Pass - parties have gotten off-track

before.approach: From the road-end parking on Forest Road 2419 (off North Lake Cushman Road/FR-24), shared with the standard route, walk the old roadbed past the standard route's trail entrance to just beyond the Big Creek crossing (~3,100 ft); a way trail leads to the base of the southeast ridge's rock section. Follow an old roadbed across Big Creek and a climbers' trail up a rock rib, gaining roughly 1,600 ft to a bowl below the Shield Wall; a gully ascends up and left to a notch at the wall's left corner (~4,850 ft) where the technical climbing begins.
what_to_bring: early start supplies for a full daylight day

watch_out: Cedar Creek can become un-fordable after hot weather increases snowmelt — one party was forced to split up and camp separately when the creek proved too dangerous to cross as a group.
Snow conditions on the couloir vary from soft and easy to hard ice depending on recent freeze-thaw — carry crampons and an axe, and consider a second tool when it is icy.
pro_tips: This couloir has been skied in good snow years.
Following an existing GPX track (several are shared by past climbers) significantly eases the trail-less sections west of Cedar Creek.
Staying just west of the creek on the approach minimizes bushwhacking.
before.descent_text: From the summit, talus-hop back down the north ridge to the head of the couloir, then descend the snow by ski, glissade, or plunge-step depending on conditions and party equipment — one party describes boot-skiing scree to bypass icy sections before a long glissade/buttslide lower down where the slope softens and mellows.

pro_tips: Keep to the described Class 3 option on the ridge if you want to avoid the harder Class 4 moves.
This traverse is more time-consuming than it looks on the map — the connecting talus between the two summits is described as requiring significant time to cross.
watch_out: Rock quality on the ridge is generally solid but still loose in spots — test holds.
The final summit step is the same lichen-slicked crux as the standard route.

Spider Gap glacier travel: moats and crevasses, ice axe required
pro_tips: Combine with Lyman Lakes peaks
Plan multiple days for access
A harder alternative approaches from Cloudy Peak (~1.5 mi one-way) via Class 3-4 climbing on its east ridge, or by dropping around a cliff band south of Cloudy's summit.

watch_out: The summit spur trail is unsigned and easy to lose in poor visibility — don't wander off the PCT onto random scree
Blocks near the summit are loose underfoot; test holds before weighting them
The natural rock arch near the summit is a scenic landmark but the ground around it is loose and exposed — watch footing while photographing it
before.approach: From the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (end of FR-2150, elev. ~4,600 ft), start on Trail 96 (Snowgrass Flat Trail). The first stretch climbs gently through forest, crossing Goat Creek on a footbridge at about 1.9 miles. Around 2.4-2.6 miles in you'll hear and then reach the springs that form the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right - the last reliable, easy water source before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek itself; there's no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except during heavy snowmelt, when it can run fast enough to require care. Just beyond the ford (~3.9-4 miles, ~5,800 ft) the trail breaks out of forest into the open heather meadows and wildflower bogs of Snowgrass Flat, a scenic rest and water-filter stop before the climb — note that camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself under Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)); parties camp instead at designated sites above/below the flats. Stay left on Trail 96 where the Bypass Trail 97 forks right toward Cispus Basin at about 3.9 miles, and continue straight past the Trail 86 junction (left, to Goat Lake) at about 4.7 miles, staying on the main track as it climbs in long benches with Mount Adams and the Goat Rocks opening up behind you. At about 5.4 miles the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 6,400 ft; turn left (north) onto the PCT. Follow the PCT north for about 1.8 miles, traversing rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill terrain on Old Snowy's west flank - snow patches can linger here into midsummer and may require an ice axe/traction for a secure traverse in early season. Watch for an unmarked climbers' path branching right (east) off the PCT toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge; take it and switchback steeply uphill for about a half mile. Many parties stash poles here for the final scramble: the last few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers. Total one-way distance is approximately 7.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain; round trip is roughly 15.5 miles, typically taking 8.5-9.5 hours car to car.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through August, tapering into a good but cooling window in September — to September.

July.reason: Snow is melting out per the best-season start; early July can still have lingering snow slopes on the ridge requiring an axe.

June.reason: Likely still holds substantial snow on approach and summit slopes; the snow-slope hazard is most acute here, and access roads may still be snow-blocked or just opening.

August.reason: Most snow-free, most stable trail conditions, and the peak crowd window — best balance of safe conditions against the highest traffic of the season.

September.reason: End of the best-season window; drier scree, fewer thunderstorms, but shorter days and increasing chance of early-season snow/weather resets late in the month.

watch_out: Loose blocks and ball-bearing scree underfoot on the talus field
Cliff bands if you stray off the SW slope/ridge line
Rapid weather changes typical of exposed Pasayten ridgelines
before.approach: Trailhead: Slate Pass (~6,900 ft), the end of the Harts Pass Road (FR-5400) just below Slate Peak lookout — this is a full backpack approach, not a day hike (~13 miles/1,400+ ft one-way to base camp, within the ~28-mile round trip). From Slate Pass, drop off the pass on the old trail/way-trail toward the Whistler Cutoff Trail; this initial descent can hold snow well into summer (some parties carry an ice axe for it). The Whistler Cutoff Trail is an easy, well-graded downhill cruise to the Middle Fork Pasayten River, which is crossed unbridged — typically only ankle-to-shin deep in normal summer flow, but ford with care during early-season snowmelt or after rain. From the ford, join the Robinson Creek / Eureka Creek Trail system and follow it roughly to the Fred's Lake cutoff around the 9-10 mile mark; trail tread is in generally good, brush-free condition to this point. At the Shellrock Trail junction the maintained tread ends — travel beyond here is on a rougher, sometimes brushy path with blowdown. Climb past Fred's Lake to 7,100-ft Rolo (Fred's) Pass, then descend/contour a short, sometimes cliff-banded slope (route-find carefully here) into the Lake Doris basin (6,975 ft), a good camp with reliable water and the standard base camp for Osceola. From camp, leave the trail and go cross-country roughly 0.6 mile northeast through open forest, then talus, gaining about 1,400 ft up Osceola's long southwest-facing scree/talus slope to either the southwest ridge or south face. The south face is a slow, tedious boulder/talus slog; a faint but real climbers' trail on the southwest ridge (roughly 48.828, -120.583) offers noticeably better footing and is preferred by parties who've found it. Final scrambling to the 8,584 ft summit is Class 2-3. Watch for wet, lichen-covered rock on the upper slope, which gets slick fast in any moisture.
pro_tips: Aim for the crest of the southwest ridge rather than grinding straight up the direct talus line — several parties report it's easier on the legs and faster
Camp at Lake Doris or near Shellrock Pass to combine Osceola with Mount Carru and/or Mount Lago on the same trip
Move deliberately and focus on foot placement on the talus — ankle injury from loose rock is the main real risk on this route
before.descent_text: Walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling on this route (rappels: 0). Descend the same southwest-ridge climbers' trail or south-face talus/scree line used on the ascent back down to Lake Doris camp (about 1,400 ft of descent, roughly an hour); the ridge line is preferred over the direct south-face boulder field for better footing, especially on wet rock. From Lake Doris, reverse the full approach: climb back over 7,100-ft Rolo/Fred's Pass (mind the cliff-banded section just above the lake), pass Fred's Lake, pick up the Eureka/Robinson Creek Trail and Whistler Cutoff Trail, re-ford the Middle Fork Pasayten River, and climb back up to Slate Pass — roughly 13 miles and a full day's hiking each way, so most parties treat this as a 2-3 day backpack rather than a car-to-car push. No technical gear is needed for the descent beyond normal scrambling caution on loose scree and any lingering snow near Slate Pass.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (useful for approach snowfields into early July)
Trekking poles for talus and scree
Sturdy boots with good ankle support
Topo map/GPS — much of the route is cross-country travel
Satellite communicator or PLB (no cell coverage in the basin)

before.approach: Park at the Lake Serene Trailhead (from Hwy 2 ~21 mi east of Monroe, turn onto FR 6020, then FR 6020-109; Northwest Forest Pass required, two outhouses at the lot) and start up Lake Serene Trail #1068, a well-graded, heavily-used maintained trail through second-growth forest. At roughly 1.6 miles a signed junction splits off a short spur to Bridal Veil Falls — stay right/uphill for Lake Serene. Shortly after, the trail crosses Bridal Veil Creek on a long footbridge (last easy, reliable water before the lake) and begins a sustained set of switchbacks, gaining about 1,900 ft over the next two miles. Around 3.5 miles and ~1,920 ft of gain (roughly 2-2.5 hrs at a moderate pace) the trail levels out at Lake Serene's outlet, marked by a toilet/outhouse sign — this is where the maintained tread ends and the scramble begins. There is no established bootpath up Philadelphia: most parties backtrack a couple hundred feet down the trail, then cut uphill into a brushy boulder field on the south side of the lake (the first ~50 ft is the worst of it) to gain the ridge above the lake's south shore. Follow that ridge crest southeast, trending close to the cliff edge above the lake (exposed, view-heavy but with real fall potential) before the angle eases through forest thick with slide alder, blowdown, and moss-slick rock. At about 3,200 ft the ridge bends east and merges into the broader west ridge of Philadelphia Mountain — a mostly timbered, Class 2 walk with a few small meadow openings — which climbs the final ~1,000 ft over roughly a mile of undulating, multi-false-summit terrain to the flat, viewless top (4,258 ft). Hazards: no path or cairns to follow (route-finding is entirely on the party), dense brush and downed timber low on the ridge, mossy rock that's slick when wet, and lingering snow into late spring — many parties intentionally time this climb for a continuous snowpack specifically to bury the brush, which trades bushwhacking for steeper, more exposed snow travel above the lake and minor avalanche/cornice considerations on that slope. Partway up the west ridge, work around a cliff band by trending left (north) rather than pushing straight through it — the cliffs are on the south side of this upper ridge, and this is the spot parties most often get stuck. Note that the handedness flips at the bend: lower down, the drop is on the north, into the lake.
pro_tips: Consider the Nov-Apr window rather than mid-summer: several trip reports specifically recommend it as a winter/early-spring snowshoe objective once snow has bridged the worst of the brush.
Leave the Lake Serene Trail near the outhouse/trail-end area at the lake and favor the north side of the ridge for periodic views of the Monte Cristo group, Gunn Peak, and Merchant Peak.
Go on a weekday if possible — the shared Lake Serene Trailhead lot is one of the busiest on the US 2 corridor on weekends.
watch_out: No trail beyond Lake Serene — losing the line through blowdown and brush is the most common way parties get slowed or turned around

A cliff band interrupts the upper west ridge; trend left/north around it rather than climbing straight up into it — the cliffs are on the south side, and the exposure lower down above the lake is on the opposite hand
Lake Serene Trailhead parking fills early on weekends since it's shared with one of the region's most popular day hikes
Northwest Forest Pass is required and not always available for purchase on-site — bring one

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: April-May, while the snow is still deep enough to walk over the brush; winter ascents on snowshoes also go

July.reason: The snow is usually gone by now, so the off-trail climb above the lake turns into a slow bushwhack through dense brush and forest, even though the ground is dry

June.reason: Lingering snow patches possible on the upper ridge in higher-snow years, and brush is leafing out and at its thickest, compounding the already-brushy approach

August.reason: Driest month, but with no snow cover the route above the lake is a full bushwhack through the thickest brush of the year, and afternoon thunderstorms are most common now

October.reason: Early snow or sustained rain can arrive, wet brush and rock significantly slow and add risk to the already loose, routefinding-heavy terrain

September.reason: Stable weather and cooler temps typical, brush begins dying back which can ease travel, but shorter days trim margin for a long brushy day

watch_out: The 'easy scramble' label undersells a couple of Class 2 moves near the summit with real exposure - watch footing on wet heather and loose rock
Dogs are prohibited on all Mount Rainier NP trails
Stay on the boot path/trail - the route runs near Research Natural Area closures protecting fragile subalpine terrain

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through September-July-October season

July.reason: Season opens mid-month; early July can still hold snow in shaded gullies on this south-aspect route, improving through the month

August.reason: Driest, most stable conditions; south aspect fully melted out, loose rock and brush at their most manageable

October.reason: Tail end of season window; early snow, rain, and shorter daylight increase routefinding and exposure risk on the off-trail sections

watch_out: No maintained trail above Rainy Lake — carry a map/compass or GPS track
Creek crossings and the climbers' path can be snow-covered and hard to find into June
Long day (11-13 mi RT, ~5,000+ ft gain) — plan turnaround time accordingly
what_to_bring: ice axe — firm spring/early-summer snow on the upper ridge
before.descent_text: This is a walk-off/scramble-down, not a rappelling route — no fixed anchors or rope work are used on the standard line. Reverse the ascent line exactly: off the summit, follow the ridge north back to the 5,800 ft saddle, then descend north-northwest off the ridge to the small tarn/bench at 5,200 ft, staying well back from any cornice edge if there is snow. From the tarn, drop back down the open slopes and skirt the cliff bands on the lake (west) side of the ridge as before, downclimbing the short rock band around 3,700 ft with care (the single spot on this route with real exposure), then pick up the Rainy Creek climbers' path back down through the brush to the Pratt Connector Trail and out to the Middle Fork Trailhead. Descent time is roughly 3.5-4 hours (about 1.5 hours from summit to Rainy Lake, 2+ hours from the lake back to the car), reflecting the loose talus, brush, and route-finding on the way down being as slow as the way up. Descent-specific hazards: the mossy slab and rock band near 3,700 ft are more consequential to downclimb than to ascend and are the likeliest spot for a slip; the boot path is easy to lose in failing light or fog since it's unofficial and unmarked; and in early/mid season, lingering snow on the upper slopes plus possible cornicing on the summit ridge call for caution and, if conditions warrant, an ice axe.
before.approach: Start at the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Trailhead (large lot at the end of FR 56). From the parking area, follow the Middle Fork Trail a short distance and cross the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River on the footbridge, then pick up the Pratt River/Pratt Connector Trail heading west/southwest — an easy, well-graded stretch of roughly 0.6 mile. Watch for the unsigned, unofficial Rainy Creek climbers' path branching off near the Rainy Creek crossing (easy to miss; GPS or a downloaded track helps here since it is not an official maintained trail). This boot path climbs steadily and steeply alongside Rainy Creek, crossing a couple of side streams/seasonal drainages around 3,100 ft — cross here rather than following the valley bottom, then angle south into steadily steepening forest to about 3,600 ft. Around 3,700 ft a short rock band forces a ~100 ft scramble move before you can side-hill in to Rainy Lake (3,800 ft), roughly 3.5-3.75 miles and 2-2.5 hours from the trailhead. The path is boot-trodden, muddy, and brushy in spots (salmonberry/blueberry brush and occasional blowdown), and largely disappears under snow through late spring — expect route-finding by feel/GPS above the lake. Rainy Lake itself is the last reliable water source. From the lake, leave the path entirely and climb the ridge that rises east then curves south above the lake's east shore, staying on the lake side (right/west side of the ridge crest) to skirt cliff bands near 4,200-4,800 ft; brushy at first, opening into slabby, mossy terrain and then open slopes above ~4,800 ft. Continue up to a flat bench with a small unnamed tarn at about 5,200 ft, then climb south to gain the summit ridge at a saddle around 5,800-5,924 ft with views down the whole Middle Fork valley, finishing with a short, straightforward ridge walk south to the 5,924 ft summit. Total is roughly 6-6.5 hours and 9.5-10 km (about 6 mi) one-way to match the ~19.3 km / 5,200 ft round trip; slab can be slick when wet, and cornices can build along the final summit ridge in winter/spring conditions.
pro_tips: Combine with a visit to the Snoqualmie Lake basin
Expect some off-trail navigation to find the best line
Ignore older route notes describing a Taylor River/Snoqualmie Lake Trail approach — current guides consistently use the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Trailhead/Rainy Creek approach instead.

what_to_bring: Satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) — cell service is unreliable to nonexistent
Extra food/fuel buffer in case weather forces a layover
A few optional pieces for the Class 3 rock finish (not essential)

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late June to mid-August, while snow bridges the Borealis Glacier and before it goes to bare ice

May.reason: Snow reaches low on Lucky Ridge and the glacier is well covered, but Thunder Creek starts rising with melt and avalanche slopes loom above.

July.reason: The Lucky Ridge path is mostly snow-free and crevasses on the Borealis Glacier are still bridged and easy to read.

June.reason: Long daylight and a well-bridged glacier; Thunder Creek runs high with snowmelt, so ford it in the morning before it rises.

August.reason: Lower creek levels ease the Thunder Creek ford; crevasses and moats open through the month, so stay on the glacier's eastern margin.

October.reason: Bare, broken glacier, new snow on loose rock, and short days for a 2-3 day remote trip with a long off-trail descent.

September.reason: The glacier turns to bullet ice with exposed crevasses and loose rock near Lucky Pass, and fall storms can shut the short window.

pro_tips: Camp at the toe of the Borealis Glacier (~6,000 ft) rather than pushing for the summit car-to-car — it turns a brutal 19-mile/7,300-ft day into a much safer overnight.
Climb early season (July) for the most solid snow bridges; by September the glacier is bare and thin.
From Lucky Pass it's an easy add-on to tag Tricouni Peak (8,102 ft) on the same trip.
Budget at least 3 days and strong glacier travel skills — this is one of the more remote Bulger List summits in the state.
Commonly combined with Austera, Klawatti, and/or Tricouni Peaks on an Inspiration/Isolation Traverse rather than climbed as a standalone objective.
Probe every snow bridge on the North Klawatti/McAllister crossing in August/September conditions.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through August; conditions can hold into early September in a good year

July.reason: Matches the best-season window; snow bridges over crevasses are typically still well consolidated early-to-mid month

August.reason: Prime climbing month - glacier generally most stable and bergschrund most manageable

September.reason: Crevasses and bergschrund open up further and snow bridges deteriorate as summer progresses; early-season snowfall can arrive by late month

before.descent_text: From the summit, the standard descent drops down the north side of Prusik Peak via a sequence of rappels, then traverses back to Prusik Pass to rejoin the approach line. Most parties make four rappels, then downclimb loose 3rd-class ground; one or two optional extra rappels can replace that downclimb - the first anchor is typically right at your feet on a flat spot at/near the true summit, with subsequent stations found by rappelling roughly 20-30m and looking climber's-left; anchors are fixed gear (slings/webbing 'tat' and rap rings/chains left by parties over the years, not bolted), so back them up or inspect carefully. Rappel lengths run mostly in the 25-30m range with one shorter first pitch; a single 60m rope is adequate for every station for a party of two, though a doubled 60m (30m per strand) can feel tight on the last traverse-y rappel, and parties of three often prefer a 70m rope for margin. After the last rappel, traverse west (skiers'-left) across talus back to Prusik Pass at the base of the West Ridge - this is not a walk-off from the summit itself, but the technical descent is short (well under an hour for an efficient party) and feeds directly back into the approach trail. From Prusik Pass, reverse the approach: down into the upper Enchantment Basin, back up and over the rim, then down the loose, steep Aasgard Pass gully to Colchuck Lake (use extra caution here - the scree that makes for a grueling ascent is equally unpleasant and slip-prone descending with tired legs), and out the Colchuck Lake/Stuart Lake Trail to the trailhead.
