before.approach: From Twisp, take Highway 20 south ~2 miles to WA-153, then south on WA-153 to County Rd 1029 (Gold Creek Loop), continuing onto County Rd 1034 (Gold Creek Road), which becomes Forest Road 4340 after about 6 miles. Turn onto FR 4340-300 (Crater Creek Road) and follow it about 4.6 miles to the Crater Creek Trailhead (~4,750 ft; day-use fee $5, or $30/yr — Northwest Forest Pass/interagency passes accepted). Hike the Crater Creek/Crater Lakes Trail about 3.9 miles one-way, gaining roughly 2,100 ft, to Lower Crater Lake (about 6,840 ft), then continue off-trail up the southeast ridge to the ~8,000 ft col and on to the summit.
pro_tips: In winter, budget heavily for the approach itself: the documented January ascent needed 8 miles of skinning on the unplowed Gold Creek/FR 4340 road plus 4 more miles of trail-breaking just to reach the trailhead area.
Camping at Crater Lake splits the trip into two manageable days rather than one very long summit push.
This side sees far less traffic than the Libby Lake gully route, so expect more route-finding and less of a boot-path.
watch_out: Upper-mountain boulders are often only lightly snow-covered even in winter, so scrambling skill (not just skis/snowshoes) is still needed near the summit.
No official winter parking/snow park exists at the Crater Creek trailhead — the unplowed road itself can be the crux of a winter attempt.
Extremely loose talus and active rockfall throughout the ~900-ft ascent gully — helmet essential.
An exposed, no-fall Class 4 move guards the true (east) summit block.
Afternoon thunderstorms are common on hot East Cascades summer days.
Mosquitoes can be intense near Libby Lake and the old cabin in early-to-mid summer.
Trail sections between roughly miles 0.8 and 2.5 have burned-out root holes from the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire.
pro_tips: Stay on the climber's-left (more solid) side of the ascent gully to reduce rockfall risk to yourself and anyone below.
USGS maps mislabel the western 'Libby' summit as the high point (8,580 ft); the true summit is the eastern peak at 8,572 ft — don't stop at the first high point reached.
Combine with neighboring Hoodoo Peak via the connecting ridge for a bigger day, but be ready for a long exposed Class 4 section and a 5.7 overhanging boulder problem on that link.
Visit in late September/early October for golden larch color along the Libby Lake Trail.

pro_tips: Good glissading on the descent when snow is present on the upper slopes
Check current trail conditions before committing — the Reynolds Creek Trail has gone multiple seasons without a chainsaw/brushing crew, leading to significant deadfall
The South Fork Reynolds Creek basin variant (SE snowfield to the east ridge) gives an easier, more consistent Class 2-3 finish than the direct saddle line
Also climbed as a winter ski-mountaineering objective via the SE basin and a narrowing summit gully — expect mixed 4th-class rock/snow near the top and check for avalanche debris after storms.

before.approach: In deep winter, park at the SR 20 closure gate (typically near the Ross Dam Trailhead) and walk/ski the closed highway to the Happy Creek area. In spring, when WSDOT has plowed several additional miles toward Happy Creek, park at the Happy Creek Nature Trail lot directly.
pro_tips: This is reportedly the least demanding way up Ruby Mountain in the right winter/spring conditions.
Wait for WSDOT to plow a few extra miles of SR 20 toward Happy Creek in spring — it substantially shortens the approach versus starting from the main winter gate.
Established skin/boot tracks from other parties make the upper open terrain considerably easier to navigate.
watch_out: The boulder field below treeline is hazardous — risk of punching through and twisting an ankle — without adequate snow cover
The skin track/bootpath has been reported steep, frozen, and low-traction in cold conditions
Avalanche potential on open upper terrain during the Cascades' wet, heavy snow events
Short but genuinely exposed knife-edge section of ridge between the col and the summit block
Scree/talus is notoriously loose underfoot — expect a slow, gritty descent by late summer rather than good scree-skiing
Trailhead road access is unreliable year to year due to washouts/landslides; confirm current status before driving up
pro_tips: Combine with Emerald Peak (a short side trip over the same col) and, for a bigger day, Cardinal Peak, for the classic three-summit Entiat Bulgers outing
Camp at Fox Camp near the Pyramid Creek Trail junction, or push about 1.5 mi farther to the larch-meadow camp directly under the Emerald-Saska col for a much shorter summit morning
Carry a helmet for the loose rock in the basin/ridge and an ice axe if climbing before mid-July, when snow often lingers in the col

An alternate, longer approach climbs from Lucerne (via the Lake Chelan ferry and Domke Lake Trail) over Emerald Park to Saska Pass — used mainly by parties combining Saska with Pinnacle Mountain, though this line has poor rock and heavy scree.
before.approach: Standard access is the North Fork Entiat River Trail (#1437) from the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (el. ~3,940 ft, at the end of Forest Road 5606, about 35.3 mi from the town of Entiat via Entiat River Road/Forest Road 51 then FR 5606). The trail crosses old fire-damaged forest with blowdown for its first miles, enters Glacier Peak Wilderness at about mile 4 (free self-issue wilderness permit, filled out at the trailhead kiosk), and reaches the Pyramid Creek/Fern Lake trail junction roughly 7-9 miles in depending on trip reports and current trailhead access (road washouts have periodically forced parties to start several miles below the official trailhead — check current Forest Service alerts). From the junction, the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail climbs west about 1,000 ft over roughly 1-1.5 miles into the high basin between Emerald and Saska; most parties camp either at Fox Camp near the junction or push on to a larch-meadow camp directly beneath the Emerald-Saska col for a shorter summit day.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September; late July-August is the most reliable stretch once the col and approach basins have shed most snow

July.reason: Snow typically lingering in the Emerald-Saska col and shaded gullies early in the month; conditions firm up by mid-to-late July

August.reason: Most reliable month - col and approach basins typically snow-free, stable dry-scramble conditions, though afternoon thunderstorms are a known hazard

September.reason: Still climbable and often quieter, but shorter days and increasing chance of early-season snow/weather at this elevation

before.approach: Drive Cascade River Road roughly 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the small, unsigned Boston Basin pulloff/trailhead at about 3,200-3,300 ft (a rough, sometimes rutted gravel road best driven with a bit of clearance). From the trailhead, follow the old abandoned mining road for about 0.75 mile to a derelict mine site, where the road ends and an unmaintained but well-traveled climbers' boot path takes over. This path climbs steeply through forest, crossing four small streams/seasonal creeks (reliable water in early/mid season, so top off bottles here), and reaches treeline around 5,300 ft after roughly 2.5-3 miles and about 3,000 ft of gain. Low camp sits on heather benches around 5,300-5,700 ft; a higher camp on a knoll above green meadows at roughly 6,300-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day. From high camp, contour up open talus and slabs to the western edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Col. Rope up for glacier travel and traverse east along the top of the glacier several hundred feet to the base of the gully/couloir below the tower - if a bergschrund or seracs bar the direct line, class 3-4 slabs on the left provide an alternate entry, rejoining the couloir about 100 ft up. Getting into the correct gully matters: on July 10, 2005, a six-person Mountaineers party mistakenly climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully here; during the roped traverse back toward the standard line a climber was struck by rockfall, and minutes later, during the retreat rappel, a natural boulder anchor gave way, killing three and seriously injuring a fourth, so confirm the line (ideally with GPS track or beta photos) before committing, especially in poor visibility. For the Southeast Face specifically, there is no separate approach line to the face itself - parties climb the first two pitches of the Southeast Ridge (the block/dihedral pitch to the notch, described in that route) and rappel from a fixed anchor at the top of pitch 2 to reach the base of the Southeast Face's crack pitch.
pro_tips: The P1 anchor is 2 bolts with no chains or rings — bring a rap ring, quicklink, or be prepared to leave a biner/sling.
There's an unhangered bolt at the base of P1; the belayer should build a supplemental gear anchor rather than rely on it alone.
Solid granite and a great, exposed position make this a highly regarded moderate-hard outing despite its short length.
before.descent_text: Descent is a combination of short technical rappels off the face followed by the shared Sharkfin descent gully used by all routes on the tower. From the top of the Southeast Face's second pitch, make two 75-foot (~23m) rappels back down to the notch atop Southeast Ridge pitch 1/2 - a single 60m rope doubled is more than adequate for both. The anchors here are bolted but sparse: the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 has no chains or rap rings, so plan to leave a locking biner, rap ring, or short cord unless you can retrieve gear on the way down; there is no anchor at the very base of pitch 1, so keep the team roped/attentive on that stretch. Once back at the ridge notch, continue down via the same downclimb-and-rappel gully system used to descend the Southeast Ridge (see that route's descent for detail) - expect several more short rappels on natural anchors (chockstones, boulders, occasional slung horns) interspersed with 3rd/4th-class downclimbing, dropping back onto the Quien Sabe Glacier and the walk back to camp. Loose rock in this gully is a real hazard, and this is where a well-documented, fatal accident occurred on July 10, 2005 (a party that had mistakenly entered this gully was retreating when a natural boulder anchor gave way about 10 feet into the rappel, sending three climbers and the boulder roughly 300 ft down the gully and killing them), so back up questionable anchors, rappel one at a time where the gully is confined, and don't over-trust a single boulder or flake.

before.approach: Start at the Park Butte Trailhead (elev. ~3,360 ft) at the end of Forest Service Road 13, reached via the Baker Lake Highway/Sulfur Creek Road turnoff (do not repeat the drive-in here — this covers the hike only). From the trailhead register, follow Park Butte Trail #603 south into Schriebers Meadow. The trail crosses Sulfur Creek on a footbridge just past the trailhead; at about 0.7 mile it crosses Rocky Creek — braided, silty glacial melt in a boulder field that can run high and fast on warm afternoons, usually bridged by a seasonal footbridge from about July. Beyond the creek the trail climbs through timber and brushy avalanche-path terrain, crosses a couple of additional meltwater streams, then switchbacks up a forested slope into Morovitz Meadows (~2 miles in). Near the meadow, stay left at the signed junction with the Scott Paul Trail #603.1 (which splits right) to stay on Park Butte Trail, then take the next right fork onto the Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 toward Baker Pass/the glacier (straight ahead leads to the Park Butte lookout instead). Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 climbs onto the crest of a narrow lateral moraine left by the receding Easton Glacier — a distinctive, uniformly graded ridge (hence the name) with exposed, steep drop-offs on both sides in places; use care in wind or on icy/frosty mornings. Designated Railroad Grade camps sit at 2.25–2.75 miles from the trailhead; High Camp sites are at about 3.75 miles and 5,600 ft; Sandy Camp, at roughly 5,900 ft, marks the end of maintained tread. From Sandy Camp the route continues cross-country over snowfields and rocky moraine to the toe of the Easton Glacier, typically 3–4 hours car-to-camp for most parties. Rope up for glacier travel around 6,800–7,200 ft (conditions-dependent) and ascend the Easton Glacier heading north toward the Sherman Crater rim; the standard line stays east (climber's right) of the glacier's major crevasse bands, though route-finding through the crevasse field is the technical crux of the approach and shifts season to season — wanding the route is standard practice given frequent whiteout/cloud cap conditions on Baker's south side. Above roughly 9,600–9,800 ft the route skirts the rim of Sherman Crater, where active fumaroles vent sulfurous steam (occasionally noticeable by smell and visible venting) — stay on the established boot path here and keep gear away from the acidic, degraded rock near the vents. No potable water exists at the trailhead itself; plan on treating water from Sulfur/Rocky Creek near the start or from snowmelt at High/Sandy Camp.
pro_tips: Treat the sulfur fumarole zone as an active hazard, not scenery — don't linger downwind or descend directly into the crater bowl

This is almost always tacked on as a bonus side-trip while climbing Baker's true summit (Grant Peak), not attempted as a standalone objective — budget the extra time for the rim detour into your turnaround plan
Wash gear and clothing after the trip — sulfuric acid residue from the crater rock corrodes fabric and metal over time.
before.descent_text: This is a glacier walk-up/scramble with no fixed rappel stations anywhere on the standard line — descent is a walk-off, reversing the ascent route. From the Sherman Peak/crater-rim high point, downclimb the summit snow slope and the West Ridge back to the crater rim first — most parties find this the psychologically hardest part of the day simply because of the steep snow right below the summit; face-in plunge-stepping or a careful glissade (only when runout and snow conditions are safe, and never near crevasses or the crater's exposed rock) is typical. Continue back down through the Sherman Crater rim area, staying alert for the same fumarole/loose-rock hazard noted on the approach, then re-rope for the descent back through the Easton Glacier's crevasse field, following your ascent wands/tracks rather than freelancing a new line, since crevasse bridges can fail or shift through the day. Below the glacier's toe, pick up the Railroad Grade moraine-crest trail back to Sandy/High Camp and down through Morovitz Meadows to the Park Butte Trailhead, re-crossing Rocky Creek near the end. In good visibility this is a straightforward reverse of the route; in Baker's characteristic cloud cap or whiteout conditions, GPS/wands become essential since the moraine crest and crater rim offer little natural handrail. There is no roped rappelling on this route in normal conditions.

before.approach: Approach from the Schriebers Meadow Trailhead (~3,366 ft) as for the Easton Glacier route, branching onto the Squak Glacier line rather than the Railroad Grade/Easton line; high camp is commonly established around 6,500 ft.
watch_out: A maze of crevasses around 8,700 ft requires careful roped route-finding on the ascent.
The summit ridge can be heavily rimed and icy outside peak summer conditions, requiring front-pointing with no fall tolerance.
Wet loose avalanches have been triggered on the descent slopes in documented trip reports — assess snow stability before descending steep terrain.
pro_tips: A large bergschrund guards the base of the final summit slopes on the Squak approach and has produced reported 50-100 ft falls onto ice — assess snow-bridge quality carefully before committing.
Some parties descend by skiing off the north side of the peak and contouring around the bergschrund rather than reversing the ascent line directly.

watch_out: Loose, sandy rock on the traverse benches below the southwest face
Crux pitch (5.4) is short but exposed with limited pro
Descent rappel pulls can be tricky - carry extra webbing/cord
pro_tips: Bivy in the basin to shorten summit day.
Weave the easiest line up the ridge.
Save rope work for the summit block.
Set an early turnaround given the long exit.
The 5.4 crux above the cave belay goes either right via a finger/hand crack into a chimney, or left on face holds with a mantle into a gully — both reach the summit ridge.

before.approach: Park along Forest Road 9070 where it meets the Pacific Crest Trail at a saddle (about 3,800 ft), roughly six miles from Hyak. Walk the PCT south for about 1.7 miles to a cairned side trail that doubles back uphill; a tarn on your left means you overshot it. The side path climbs about 0.3 mile with a few class 2-3 moves to Abiel Pass, the saddle between Tinkham and Silver peaks, where the scramble up the summit slopes begins.

Follow the same multi-day approach as the Southwest Route to a high camp on Itswoot Ridge or near the Dome Glacier, then continue over the Dome-Chickamin Glacier col (~8,500 ft) and descend onto the Chickamin Glacier, traversing beneath Sinister's north side to reach the base of the face. The original 1980 first ascent instead approached from the Blizzard-Gunsight col, traversing the Chickamin Glacier from the west.
watch_out: Bergschrund crossing near the base of the face
Icefall/serac hazard — climbers have observed house-size ice blocks calved from Sinister's slopes onto the Chickamin Glacier below
Afternoon thunderstorms are common in the North Cascades in summer

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: June to early July, while the face holds firm snow over the ice and the bergschrund at its base is still filled

May.reason: A filled bergschrund and firm snow, but a long snowbound approach over the Dome-Chickamin col and a real spring avalanche cycle.

July.reason: Good early in the month; by late July the snow thins toward ice near the steepest pitch and the bergschrund opens.

June.reason: Firm snow on the 45-50 degree face, a filled bergschrund and bridged crevasses on the Chickamin Glacier approach.

April.reason: The face can be in good snow with the bergschrund filled, but the approach is buried and exposed to avalanches for days.

August.reason: The face bares to hard alpine ice, the bergschrund widens and rockfall and icefall from the upper slopes increase.

September.reason: Bare ice, an open bergschrund and heavy rockfall; the glacier approach is a maze of open crevasses.

pro_tips: Standard access to Skookum is from the east via Elbow Lake Trail #697 and the Green Creek climbers' path — not the Dailey Prairie/west-side roads used for North and South Twin
Confirm the Elbow Lake trailhead river crossing is actually passable before committing — the log/rope crossing washed out in the December 2025 floods and has not been rebuilt
The olivine is famously grippy (like coarse sandpaper) on the ridges but loose and rotten on south-facing slopes — pick your ascent/descent line accordingly
The north ridge stays true to the crest on bomber rock with immense exposure; a thin 30 m rope just reaches on the rappel off Jaws' Tooth.

watch_out: loose talus high on the slope
what_to_bring: Sturdy boots with good ankle support
Trekking poles for the loose descent
Map/compass or a GPS track — the route beyond Skyline Lake is an unofficial, unsigned boot path
Extra water — south-facing slopes offer little shade
Wind layer/shell for the open ridge crest
Helmet worth considering if other parties are on the loose rock above or below you

pro_tips: Time the North Fork Sauk ford for low water
Glacier is shrinking — assess bergschrund late season
Early start to beat softening snow
watch_out: river ford
crevasses
exposed summit move

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: mid-July through September, with late July-August the most reliable stretch

July.reason: ford levels start dropping and the corkscrew usually clears of snow by mid-month, matching the best-season start

June.reason: North Fork Sauk typically runs high with snowmelt, and residual snow can still cover parts of the corkscrew and approach trail

August.reason: lowest, safest river crossing and driest rock on the upper scramble; most trip reports cluster here

September.reason: low water and stable rock continue, though shortening days and possible early-season snow late in the month add risk

before.approach: The North Fork Sauk approach starts from the unsigned Sloan Peak climbers'-trail pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road, reached via SR 530 south of Darrington) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk River — not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649, but a boot path a short distance further along FR 49. From the pullout the path is flat and brushy (stinging nettle, then devil's club) for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the North Fork Sauk River, which must be forded or crossed on logs (log jams are usually adequate about 0.5 mi in; they shift year to year and can be dicey in high water/early season). The path fords the river braids two to three times over the next mile, then follows Cougar Creek upstream on a faint, cairned/flagged track through sandy streambed and forest — expect route-finding to be slow here, especially with snow on the ground into early summer. Around 3,000–3,200 ft the trail crosses Cougar Creek itself (can be impassable lower down; look for a crossing around 3.2K ft) and climbs steeply through switchbacks in forest, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft (roughly 2–2.5 hrs from the car, and the last reliable water before the basin). Above the falls the climbers' path breaks out of the trees onto scree and slabs, angling up to the 5,800 ft saddle/basin on Sloan's northeast side (reached ~4–5 hrs in for most parties), with a small stream and possible campsite in the basin — the standard overnight/base camp spot for a two-day ascent. From the basin, ledges and slabs lead up to the toe of the Sloan Glacier; rope up and gear up (crampons, axe, glacier kit) here before crossing onto the ice toward the southeast edge of the summit massif. The often-preferred approach uses the Bedal Creek trailhead (FS 4096, a rough 3-mile 4WD spur off the Mountain Loop Highway, ~2,790 ft) and the old Bedal Creek trail/climbers' path to the same 5,300 ft Bedal–Sloan saddle, avoiding the North Fork Sauk fords entirely at the cost of a rougher access road; total stats by that line run about 9.5 mi and 5,300 ft round trip. Either way, expect avalanche/snow-slope hazard on the basin and glacier approach into early summer, one notable open crevasse on the Sloan Glacier that's typically snow-bridged in normal season, and generally loose, brushy, unmaintained tread below treeline on both approaches.

From Marblemount, drive Cascade River Road ~14.2 miles to the signed FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Road) junction and turn right. Cross the Cascade River on a concrete bridge and continue ~0.4 mile to a Y junction where the right fork is blocked by boulders — park here (roughly 1,150-1,300 ft; a long-standing washout on FR-1570 keeps most parties from driving any higher). A climbers' trail flagged with pink ribbon every 50-150 ft leaves the old roadbed and climbs steeply and directly through old growth — about 1,700 vertical ft in the first mile — to a ridge saddle near Point 5116. At the saddle there is an easy-to-miss junction: go left and climb roughly 1,000 ft to Peak 5791, then traverse heather benches and meadows above Cyclone Lake, crossing or contouring Peak 5860, to reach the base of Snowking's East Ridge. Figure ~5 hours and ~5,000 ft of gain from the car to the Cyclone Lake/ridge base.
watch_out: Easy-to-miss junction at the Pt. 5116 saddle — missing it puts you on the wrong ridge
Brush and deadfall low on the climbers' trail before it firms up in old growth
No cell coverage on the approach or ridge — carry a satellite communicator
Long, remote day — budget a full weekend even for fit parties

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July to early September, once the flagged trail and ridge crest are snow-free

May.reason: A long snow slog over Kindy Ridge with the flagging buried; feasible for strong parties with an axe, but avalanche-prone slopes above Cyclone Lake.

July.reason: The ridge crest and heather benches melt out and camps near Cyclone Lake have water; early July can still hold summit-block cornices.

June.reason: Mostly snow travel on the ridge and near the summit block; the pink-flagged forest trail is harder to follow where it is snow-covered.

August.reason: Snow-free benches and slabs make navigation easiest; water gets scarce high on the ridge late in the month.

October.reason: Early snow hides the flagging and slicks the ridge slabs, and daylight is short for a two-day, 6,800 ft trip.

September.reason: Dry talus and slabs with fall color, but shorter days on a 5,000-plus ft approach from the washed-out FR-1570.

pro_tips: Good bivy sites with snowmelt water sit at roughly 6,300 ft and 6,900 ft directly on the ridge, making this a comfortable two-day objective.

before.approach: Drive US-2 to Skykomish, then north on Beckler River Road (FR-65) for about 15 miles; turn left (west) onto FR-63 and follow it about 4.6 miles to where it crosses the North Fork Skykomish River again. Just past that bridge the road bends right over a small rise about a mile east of Galena (~1,150 ft); park at the unmarked roadside pullout there. Leave the road on the side away from the river and head directly, off-trail, up the steep, blowdown-choked slope toward Spire Mountain. There is no tread anywhere on the mountain: the line works around cliff bands at roughly 4,200-4,400 ft on the peak's north side, traverses southeast to about 5,400 ft below the summit spires, and gains the west/northwest ridge for the final scramble to the top. An older, historic alternate approach (Fred Beckey's original line) starts south of Index via the North Fork Skykomish River Road, which now dead-ends at a washout around mile 6, then follows the unmaintained Trout Creek Road south to reach the same ridge — a much brushier ~16-mile, ~7,000 ft round trip, longer than today's standard FR-63 approach.
pro_tips: Carry a short hand line or a few meters of rope for the ~10 ft Class 5 step at ~6,100 ft — most parties find it easier to protect than to solo
Start very early; the off-trail approach, brush, and cliff-band route-finding make for a long day even before the technical ridge
Save or download a GPS track from a recent trip report — there's no trail anywhere on the route, and threading the cliff bands is the crux of the approach, not just the summit ridge
what_to_bring: Short hand line or ~30m rope for the crux step
Sturdy boots with good edging for the ridge
GPS or offline map with a saved track
Satellite messenger or PLB (no cell coverage)
watch_out: The ridge is mostly Class 3, but two short sections are genuinely Class 4-5 — don't commit to the ridge unprepared for a real 5th-class move
The 4,200-4,400 ft cliff bands can cliff you out if you traverse too high or low — locate the described bypass before committing to a line
This is one of the least-visited Everett-area peaks; don't count on other parties, a boot path, or cell signal for help if something goes wrong

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September

July.reason: Snow-filled gullies and lingering snowpack are still common early-to-mid month; ice axe/crampons recommended; conditions improve steadily as the month progresses

August.reason: Driest, most stable window with the least residual snow in the gullies and benches - the best month for the southwest flank scramble

September.reason: Rock is dry and stable but days are shorter and early-season snow/weather can arrive late in the month, especially at this 8500+ ft elevation

what_to_bring: Bear canister or NPS-approved food storage for the multi-day approach
Satellite communicator (InReach or similar) given the lack of cell coverage
Water treatment for camps along Thunder/Park/Bridge Creek

watch_out: Don't commit to the first (left-most) snow finger without checking it reaches the south ridge — parties have had to backtrack and exit right onto scree instead
Rock on the Southeast Face slabs and upper gullies is notably loose; test holds and be mindful of parties below
Morning gully ice below the ridge notch can require crampons even in late summer
loose rock
remoteness
afternoon thunderstorms
pro_tips: Often combined with Martin Peak (and sometimes Angel Staircase) into a single Sawtooth Ridge crest traverse
Eagle Lakes/Crater Creek Trailhead's well-graded multi-use trail (shared with mountain bikes/motorbikes) offers an alternate approach angle to Cooney Lake besides Foggy Dew
before.approach: Two trailheads reach Cooney Lake and the SE Ridge. (1) Foggy Dew Trailhead (end of FR 4340-200, 3,400 ft) — from Twisp, take SR 20 east ~2 mi, then SR 153 south ~12 mi, then Gold Creek Loop Rd/County Rd 1034 and FR 4340 to the FR 4340-200 spur. Hike Foggy Dew Creek Trail #417 about 4.9 miles to its end, then Martin Creek Trail #429 north 2.7 miles and Cooney Lake Trail #434 0.2 mile to Cooney Lake (~7,200 ft); climb to Cooney Pass and the SE Ridge from there. Round trip is roughly 19 miles with about 5,560 ft of gain (a logged trip report took ~5.5 hr up, ~3 hr down). (2) Eagle Lakes/Crater Creek Trailhead (also off FR 4340, 4,700 ft) — follow the Crater Creek/Eagle Lake Trail #431 about 2.5 miles to a signed cutoff heading south toward Martin and Cooney Lakes, then 4.0 miles to Martin Lakes (6,700 ft) and 2.2 more miles to Cooney Lake (7,200 ft) to join the same summit route.

Primary approach (White River side): From Hwy 2 at Coles Corner, follow Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (Forest Road 6400) to its end at the White River/Indian Creek Trailhead (~2,300 ft). Hike the White River Trail #1507 about 6 miles to the Thunder Creek crossing. A half mile past Thunder Creek, leave the maintained trail and pick up an old, unmaintained sheep trail that climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage through avalanche debris and brush to a lower basin (~4,175 ft), then steeply up to the upper Thunder Basin (~5,180 ft, about 9 miles and 2,900 ft above the trailhead) — the standard high camp with a direct view of Tenpeak. Alternate approach (North Fork Sauk / west side): drive the Mountain Loop Highway to Forest Road 49 and the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (2,100 ft), follow North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country via Boulder Pass and the Napeequa Valley to Tenpeak's north/northeast side — a much longer, more committing option (reported as ~31 miles and 13,500 ft of gain over 3 days for a full traverse) with 20+ stream crossings and dense brush. From the Thunder Basin camp, the route continues across talus and snow to a col east of the summit block (ice axe/crampons typically needed for the sometimes-firm snow), then climbs a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system, followed by a broken chimney/face pitch (Class 4 to easy Class 5 depending on conditions) to the summit; rock in the gully and chimney is loose, so helmet up and manage rope/party spacing to avoid dropping rock on others below.
watch_out: crevasses
exposed summit block
remote committing terrain

before.approach: FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the Canyon Creek bridge, so first walk or bike roughly 8-9 miles of road to the trailhead. The climb starts at the Tupso Pass trailhead on the Three Fingers-Goat Flats-Saddle Lake Trail #641. The trail climbs through forest, crossing a couple of small seasonal streams, to Saddle Lake at about 2.5 miles (last reliable, easy water before the alpine section; no camping within 200 ft of the lake and no fires from here on). From Saddle Lake continue roughly 2–2.5 more miles, gaining out of the timber into the open meadows of Goat Flats (~4.5 mi from the TH) — good camps and the last easy tentsites with views to Puget Sound. From Goat Flats the trail contours and climbs about 2 more miles to Tin Can Gap (~6.2 mi, roughly 3,500-3,800 ft of the day's gain done); this is the last maintained-trail point and the standard high camp/bivy for peak days. Tin Can Gap gives the first real view of the three summits and the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier below. From the gap the route drops about 400 ft off-trail down snow/talus onto the glacier — early season this is a straightforward snow descent, but by late summer expect bare ice and a moat between rock and ice that requires care (crampons/axe recommended into at least July); crevasses open on the glacier by mid-summer so rope up if traveling as a team when covered. Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft on the far side to the col between Middle and North Peak — this climb is on a mix of snow/scree and low-angle rock and is the route-finding crux of the approach. From the col, the North Peak route follows a ramp leading left then angling right into a shallow chimney, with sustained 4th-class and a few low-5th-class (5.0-5.4) exposed moves through loose-to-fair rock to the summit block; a harder 5.4 line exists on the upper west face but is avoided by most parties for rock quality. Carry a rope, a small rack, and glacier gear (axe/crampons, and a rope+harness for crevasse hazard) even in a scramble-grade season.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to September

July.reason: Improves through the month as snow melts out; matches the start of the late July window

June.reason: Lingering snow slopes low on the route and near the summit steps, plus longer/harder road access

August.reason: Driest, most consolidated conditions and core of the best-season

October.reason: Outside the window — early snow and shorter weather windows increase risk on the exposed ladder section

September.reason: Still within the season; stable weather common early in the month

before.approach: FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the Canyon Creek bridge, so first walk or bike roughly 8-9 miles of road to the trailhead. Then follow the same approach as the other two summits: Trail #641 from Tupso Pass over Saddle Lake (2.5 mi) and Goat Flats (~4.5 mi) to Tin Can Gap (~6.2-7 mi), then drop ~400 ft off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier and cross it (moat and possible crevasse hazard — crampons/axe recommended, rope up if crevasses are open). Most parties bivy on or near the glacier below the peaks rather than pushing all three summits car-to-car. From a glacier-side camp, Middle Peak's south face is reached by a short climb/traverse toward the base of the peak; one detailed trip report logged the summit in about 37 minutes from a glacier bivy. The route itself is solid 3rd- and 4th-class scrambling on the lower face, transitioning to looser, more broken 3rd-class rock higher up — take care with rockfall onto anyone below, and expect the climbing to run longer than the peak's modest height suggests since the face is broader than it looks from the glacier. No technical rock gear is required for the standard line, but a rope is worth carrying for the optional short rappel on descent (see below) and in case conditions call for a belay on the looser upper section.

Same trailhead and initial trail as the East/Main Peak standard route: Mineral Creek Trailhead (2,400 ft), across the Kachess River ford, 1.7 miles of trail to the Mineral Creek crossing, then about 1 mile through vine maple brush to the base of the south-side talus slope below Middle Peak.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through mid-September, once seasonal snow has cleared from the approach gully and summit notch —-season guidance

July.reason: Approach snow is usually mostly melted by mid-to-late July, but early-July ascents can still encounter lingering snow in the gully/notch per the early-season-snow hazard

August.reason: Most reliable month for dry rock and a cleared approach; watch for the afternoon thunderstorm hazard, which peaks in August

September.reason: Stable, cooler conditions and a fully melted-out route, though shorter daylight and the first shoulder-season snow are possible late in the month

before.approach: Start at the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead (~4,875 ft) on SR-20, 4.7 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound as it switchbacks up through forest and into larch parkland to Cutthroat Pass (~6,800 ft, ~4.9 mi) — this stretch has only intermittent small streams, so fill up at the last stream below the pass, since the pass itself is dry and little reliable water exists again until Snowy Lakes. From Cutthroat Pass the PCT contours below Cutthroat Peak's west flank to Granite Pass (~6,300 ft, roughly 6.5-7 mi from the trailhead); this pass holds snow into July/August, and when snow-covered it's steep and exposed enough that an ice axe (and comfort self-arresting) is warranted. Beyond Granite Pass the trail sidehills below Tower Mountain's west side, crosses a cliff-cut, blasted-out section, and loses a bit of elevation into a meadowed basin. Roughly 9.5-10 miles in, about a mile short of Methow Pass at about 6,300 ft, a climbers'/use path branches right (east) off the PCT and climbs ~0.5 mi and ~400 ft to the Snowy Lakes basin — Lower Snowy Lake (~6,600 ft) or Upper Snowy Lake (~6,700 ft) — the standard base camp, with reliable water and good tent sites; most parties backpack in and climb from camp rather than going car-to-car. From camp near Lower Snowy Lake, head cross-country south toward Tower Mountain on a climbers' path, then make a short but strenuous traverse across a talus field, aiming for a distinctive large reddish boulder partway across. Beyond the boulder, a ramp on the left side of a large cave (which cuts about 25 yards into the mountainside and makes a good wind-sheltered rest stop) leads up to the base of the main summit gully — from here the route follows ledges on the gully's right side, zigzagging back toward the gully-notch in the ridge and up broken rock to the summit. Total distance to the base of the gully runs roughly 10-11 miles one-way with about 1,800 ft of net elevation gain from the trailhead to camp (more once the ups and downs over Cutthroat and Granite passes are counted). The gully itself is the route's main hazard: the rock is notoriously loose and rockfall-prone, so helmets are strongly recommended and parties should climb one at a time, staying right and moving efficiently through the narrowest sections.

Start at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20 (Diablo Lake, milepost 130, roughly 25 miles east of Marblemount) and park in the large lot above the boat ramp on the campground's south side — this is also the Thunder Creek Trailhead. Follow the maintained Thunder Creek Trail south about 6.5-6.7 miles to McAllister Camp (~1,900 ft), a backcountry stock camp where McAllister Creek meets Thunder Creek. The trail's original bridge over Thunder Creek near mile 6.6 washed out in fall 2017; parties now cross on logs a short way upstream of the old bridge site. Across the creek, pick up the unmaintained climbers' boot path at the first fork, climbing steeply through brush and around downed timber up the north ridge; a viewpoint near 4,600 ft gives the first look at Primus, Tricouni, and neighboring peaks. Continue through forest and heather to Borealis Lake (base camp), a flat bench below the Borealis Glacier. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and climb the Borealis Glacier, skirting the icefall in its middle — it has retreated significantly and split into upper and lower tiers separated by slabs and cliffs — navigating crevasses to Lucky Pass, the Primus-Tricouni col. From Lucky Pass, climb a steep snow finger roughly 200 ft up Tricouni's southwest side, then transition to rock ramps and ledges (class 3-4 scrambling) up the west ridge to the bouldery 8,102 ft summit. Hazards: crevasses on the Borealis Glacier (worse late season), a brushy and poorly marked boot path above McAllister Camp, and afternoon softening of the snow finger.
pro_tips: Climb together with Primus and Austera on a single glacier circuit
Cross the glacier early while bridges are frozen

before.approach: Ferry/floatplane to Stehekin (no road access), then the Company Creek Trail roughly 3 miles to a point below Tupshin's west side. Leave the trail and scramble up White Goat Mountain's west slopes through dense brush, traversing rightward through the 4,200-4,600 ft band, then cross a roughly 7,200 ft pass above Bird Lakes and descend into the Bird Lakes basin below Tupshin's east face (face starts ~7,600 ft).
watch_out: A serious, poorly-protected 5.4-5.6 crux move where a fall would be severe
Loose rock on the ledges
Snow/moat conditions lingering at the ~7,600 ft base of the face
pro_tips: Budget more time than expected for the ledge system — multiple parties describe it as slow, zigzagging route-finding
A 30 m rope has been enough for the technical sections
Some parties find an easier variation lower-angle than the crux flake — scout before committing
what_to_bring: sturdy approach shoes for brush and talus
ice axe/crampons if snow lingers on the approach traverse

watch_out: Heather approach ledges become quite slick with any moisture
Early-season parties may need an axe and crampons for steep snowfields on the approach
Watch for loose rock and lichen-covered holds, especially after freeze-thaw cycles
before.approach: Start at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (Sunrise Mine Trail #707) off the Mountain Loop Highway near Big Four/Barlow Pass. The trail begins in second-growth forest and almost immediately crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish via a log crossing that can be a genuine obstacle during high runoff (early season/after rain). From there the trail climbs steadily through Wirtz Basin, breaks out of the trees into open talus and boulder fields marked by cairns, and reaches Headlee Pass at roughly 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles in — a narrow, rocky notch/couloir with loose rock underfoot where rockfall from parties above is a real hazard. Past the pass the trail drops briefly through trees, then crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek, which it follows up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, ~4,950 ft, ~3.5 mi/~2,700 ft gain from the trailhead) — the last reliable running water before the climb. From the lake, cross the outlet and follow the summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then swing north across the slabs to the saddle/col between Vesper and Wolf Peak. From the saddle, a ledge system cuts across Vesper's north face at roughly 5,800 ft, reached by walking out steep, exposed heather benches that get slick when wet and hold a steep snow slope into early-to-mid summer (ice axe and possibly crampons recommended for that window). The ledge leads to a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier remnant, near where True Grit's start is found. Allow 3+ hours from the trailhead to the base of the route.
pro_tips: Pitch 4's splitter crack with its brief step-across is the route's namesake crux

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to early September, after the snow slope on the heather benches melts and before fall rain slicks them

July.reason: The route dries out, but early July can still hold the steep snowfield on the approach ledges; bring an axe and crampons.

June.reason: The Mountain Loop gate usually opens by late spring, but the river log crossing runs high and a steep snow slope covers the benches.

August.reason: The approach ledges are usually snow-free and the north face is dry and pleasantly shaded; Vesper Lake still offers water.

October.reason: Short days, cold rock on a north face, and slick heather after rain; the first snow can return to the approach ledges.

September.reason: Still dry in stable spells, but the north face is cold, and rain makes the heather benches and lichen-covered rock slick.

what_to_bring: Approach shoes suited to scree and heather
Ice axe and crampons for early-season snowfields on the traverse
Light rain shell (afternoon convective storms are common)

pro_tips: This is also the standard jumping-off point for Mount Challenger, so parties can combine both summits from one Perfect Pass camp
Ramps/ledges climber's-right of the summit col offer an alternative if the direct col approach looks poor
before.approach: The standard approach begins at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of Hannegan Pass Rd/FS-32 off SR 542, ~3,100 ft), following Hannegan Pass Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Hannegan Pass (~5,050-5,100 ft). From the pass, the trail switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp, then continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing — a ford that can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow and is the approach's main hazard; check levels before committing, and expect it to be harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle (~5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5-8.5 hours/8-9 miles from the trailhead depending on pace and the ford). From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest of Easy Ridge, over or around Easy Peak (6,613 ft, ascend its south ridge), to the notorious 'Imperfect Impasse' — a notch guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often-wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe or impassable; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft down to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs a exposed Class 4 rock step (many parties belay this) to regain the ridge on the far side. Beyond the Impasse the trail continues to Perfect Pass (~6,200 ft), the standard high camp for Whatcom Peak, about 16 miles in from the trailhead, commonly the end of a second day, though fast parties reach it in one. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass itself in late season — plan to fill up at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt. An alternative approach skips Easy Ridge entirely: from Whatcom Pass (reached via the Chilliwack River/Brush Creek trail or the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake — see the North Ridge route for that approach), a 'low orbit' traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields without crossing the Impasse, but it exposes climbers to the moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier and should be treated as glacier travel (rope/crevasse-rescue gear) in early season.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early October, once snow has melted off the upper slopes

July.reason: Snow typically clears from the upper gully by mid-July; long daylight and stable summer weather, though early-July ascents can still hit lingering snowfields

August.reason: Most reliable month - talus fully exposed, driest conditions, though afternoon thunderstorms are common and should be watched for

October.reason: Early season snow can return to the high pass terrain at any time, days are short, and North Cascades Highway/access conditions become less predictable

September.reason: Still generally dry and clear with fewer bugs and crowds than midsummer, but shorter daylight and first frosts begin

pro_tips: The Rainy Pass PCT-lot gully approach doubles as a well-regarded spring corn-snow ski descent — go early enough to catch the snow softening but before it turns to mush
On the south-ridge route, cutting left across gullies at ~6,800 ft onto the southwest slope avoids the harder gully scrambling higher on the ridge crest
before.approach: Two trailheads serve this scramble, both off SR-20 between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass. Option A (PCT approach, most commonly used): park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass (~4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff). From the lot, leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country/climber's-path east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs — there is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT. Continue up through the trees (expect lingering snow patches into early summer) to about 6,100 ft, where the forest opens into a meadow basin below the west ridge/gully complex. From the basin, trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder; the final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above. Round trip via this line runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain (trailhead 4,850 ft to summit 7,790 ft). Option B (highway turnout approach, reaches the true south ridge): from the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, ~5,000 ft), walk back down/along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees. Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way. This line is also about 4 miles round trip with ~3,000 ft gain. Both approaches are trail-less above the first stretch of forest — expect route-finding, loose talus/scree in the gullies, and class 2-3 terrain with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully; no reliable water source above the lower forest, so carry what you need from the car. No creek fords or avalanche paths of note on the standard summer line, but early-season snow lingers in the forest and basin and can make the gully sections firm or icy.

watch_out: No maintained trail or cairned path above camp - carry map/compass or GPS and know how to navigate open forest and heather terrain
Snow can persist on north-facing slopes and the La Crosse-White Mountain cirque into July
Dosewallips Road washout permanently adds 5.5-7 miles of road walking/biking each way - factor this into trip planning and timing
pro_tips: Bring a bike to cover the closed Dosewallips roadbed faster if approaching from the north
Reserve your wilderness permit well ahead of the trip - Olympic NP's popular season reservations open in mid-April
Check current trail/road conditions with the Wilderness Information Center before committing, since the LaCrosse Pass Trail condition and Dosewallips road status can change season to season
Camp at Marmot Lake (south approach) or Honeymoon Meadows (north approach) - both are established sites with the shortest remaining scramble to the summit

watch_out: Unmarked junction at about 0.9 mile — stay on the main climbers' trail toward the summit ridge
In 2025, parties noted two steep snow crossings on avalanche-prone slopes persisting as late as mid-July; alternate routes below both are recommended if uncomfortable on snow
The road beyond Yellow Aster Butte TH is essentially one lane with blind corners — yield to descending traffic

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through October - with the caveat that early-mid July still commonly has the steep snow traverse in place

July.reason: Steep snow often still covers the south/west traverse early in the month; ice axe and snow-travel experience recommended until it melts out, improving to good by late July

August.reason: Typically the most reliable month - trail clear of snow, wildflowers and berries out, road usually passable

October.reason: Can still be climbed but watch for early-season snow or ice returning to the traverse and the access road, plus shorter daylight windows

September.reason: Stable, dry conditions and fall colors; cooler temps and shorter days but generally the best combination of clear trail and light crowds

before.approach: From Loomis, drive Toats Coulee Road (FR-39) roughly 22 miles to Long Swamp Campground, then continue about 3 more miles west on FR-39 to the Cathedral Driveway trailhead. The final stretch of road is gravel but reported as smooth/passenger-car friendly.
watch_out: Blowdown/deadfall sections reported beyond the first creek crossing.
Sparse water — only one spring noted along this approach.
Same exposed-ridge thunderstorm risk near the summit as the standard route.
pro_tips: This is the shortest way to the true summit if you don't mind the extra few miles of driving to reach the Cathedral Driveway trailhead.
Expect some blowdown beyond the first creek crossing in less-maintained years — one party counted roughly 30 downed trees across the trail.

before.approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,300 ft, reached via Forest Road 6024 off US Highway 2 in Baring), follow Barclay Creek Trail 1055, then leave the maintained trail to bushwhack along Barclay Creek and up Tailgunner Creek to an old, overgrown logging road. A bootpath climbs through forest to about 4,000 ft, crosses a Class 2-3 waterfall ravine, then follows the Tailgunner Couloir (grass and snow patches) to Tailgunner Pass (roughly 5,320-5,360 ft), which lies WNW of the Wing Peak summit.
watch_out: The crux snowfinger below the summit is reported at roughly 70 degrees and severely exposed — a slip here would be consequential.
Loose Class 4 rock on the final summit block, especially hazardous when wet or dusted with snow.
A rock defile with deep moats below the summit snow face has been called the most unnerving part of the descent.

pro_tips: Because the approach is so long, most parties link Wolframite with other Pasayten summits (Apex, Pope, Barchester Towers, Bauerman Ridge, Arnold, Horseshoe) on one extended trip rather than making a single dedicated round trip

Aim for late July through August/early September to minimize both lingering snow and the risk of an early-season storm like the one that produced snowfall on the summit in a documented mid-October ascent

The Chewuch Trail #510 → Tungsten Creek Trail #534 approach is longer than the Andrews Creek Trail alternative but fully cleared, shadier, and passes the historic Tungsten Mine — worth the extra miles
before.approach: Park at the Thirtymile Trailhead (~3,400 ft) at the end of West Chewuch Road, about 29 miles north of Winthrop. From there follow the Chewuch River Trail #510 north, staying close to the Chewuch River; Chewuch Falls is a good landmark around 2.5 miles in. Around mile 8 to 8.8 the trail crosses a 2001 burn area — standing dead snags are common here and more prone to falling in wind, so be alert in storms. At roughly 8-8.8 miles (~4,700 ft) reach the signed junction with Tungsten Creek Trail #534, just after fording Horseshoe Creek, and turn right onto it. Follow Tungsten Creek Trail #534 for 6.2 miles, gaining about 2,100 ft, passing within earshot of Big Horn and Horseshoe Creeks and crossing Cinch Creek; Tungsten Creek itself, which the trail follows for its final stretch, is the last dependable water before the high country (in dry years, e.g. a September 2017 trip, sources beyond here were reported as dry streambeds and stagnant pools, so tank up). This trail ends at its junction with the Boundary Trail #533 at the historic Tungsten Mine Camp (~6,750 ft) — old mine structures, iron pipe, and building ruins from the 1908-1920s tungsten operation are visible on the south side of Wolframite Mountain. This point is roughly 14-15 miles in, effectively a full day's hike, and most parties camp near here rather than pushing to the summit and back in one day. From the mine camp junction, follow the Boundary Trail #533 west for about 1 mile to the point where the trail bends south toward Apex Pass. Leave the trail here and ascend off-trail, heading northeast up Wolframite's broad, gentle west slopes to the 8,136-8,137 ft summit; done on this line the terrain is a straightforward Class 2 talus/heather slope, though other lines or variations can involve short sections of low Class 3. This is the safest and most recommended line up the peak. Total one-way distance from the trailhead is roughly 16-17 miles with about 4,700 ft of cumulative gain, consistent with the ~34-mile (54.72 km) round trip — treat this as a backpack with a high camp near Tungsten Mine or the Boundary Trail, not a single-day car-to-car scramble.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September; July–August is the core dry-trail window

July.reason: Season start (mid-July); trail and off-trail slopes typically snow-free, long daylight for the long approach

June.reason: Lingering snow on north-facing terrain and high creek crossings on the long approach; trails may not be fully melted out this far north in the Pasayten

August.reason: Most reliable dry-trail, low-snow window; watch for the documented afternoon thunderstorms

October.reason: Outside the best season; early snow and freezing temps likely at 8,000+ ft this far north, plus hunting season on approach trails

September.reason: Still within the best-season window; stable weather but shorter days and rising chance of early-season snow toward late month
